data.title: Reverse NI tax raid or watch 40,000 jobs disappear, Burnham warned
data.description:
Tens of thousands of jobs in pubs, restaurants and hotels will be lost unless Andy Burnham reverses Labour’s jobs tax, hospitality bosses have warned.

UKHospitality, an industry trade body, urged the Prime Minister to back tax cuts that would benefit almost a quarter of a million jobs and help tackle Britain’s youth unemployment crisis.

The warning follows a landmark review by Alan Milburn, the former health secretary, who criticised the barrage of higher employment costs and regulations imposed on businesses.

Mr Milburn called on ministers to make it “cheaper and less risky” for businesses to hire young people, including by cutting employers’ National Insurance bills.

However, the proposals face resistance from the Treasury, despite sympathy from John Healey, the Chancellor, for efforts to tackle youth unemployment.

The trade body warned that another 40,000 hospitality jobs could disappear over the next year unless the Government reduces the cost of hiring workers.

More than 15,000 of those jobs are expected to be held by young people, worsening a crisis that has already left nearly a million 16 to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neet).

Mr Milburn proposed doubling the earnings threshold at which employers start paying the tax for workers aged 21 to 24 in hospitality, retail and leisure, from £5,000 to £10,000.

It would represent a partial reversal of Rachel Reeves’s £25bn raid announced in the former chancellor’s maiden Budget.

UKHospitality has estimated that the measure would benefit around 240,000 jobs in the sector and save businesses £170m a year.

Writing for The Telegraph, Allen Simpson, UKHospitality’s chief executive, warned that the Government risked condemning thousands more young people to unemployment unless it acted.

He said: “Let’s be clear, there is no Milburn review without the National Insurance cut it recommends. We will not get jobs for young people flowing without the high street and the high street won’t start hiring again without costs coming down.”

Mr Healey is said to be sympathetic to efforts to tackle youth unemployment, though Treasury officials are understood to be resisting plans to cut taxes for businesses hiring under-25s over concerns about the cost to the Exchequer.

However, Mr Simpson warned that refusing to act would cost the Treasury even more as young people are pushed on to benefits.

Nearly 100,000 hospitality jobs have already disappeared since Labour came to power, accounting for 45pc of all jobs lost across the economy during that period, according to the business group.

Mr Simpson said: “I would estimate, extrapolating the past two years of employment data, that we could see another 40,000 people lost from hospitality alone in the next 12 months unless we start to repair the damage. More than 15,000 of those, statistically, are likely to be young people.

“That’s more doomscrolling in bedrooms. More young people’s lives on hold and more benefits for the taxpayer to fund.”

He urged Downing Street to overrule Treasury objections and implement Mr Milburn’s recommendations.

Mr Simpson added: “This is a time for courage against intransigence. Downing Street need to face down the opponents of the review.”

The Treasury has been contacted for comment.

It simply costs too much to hire young workers

By Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality

The UK faces a Neets crisis. That much is obvious. The real question is: does the Government have the courage to make the tough decisions urged by Alan Milburn in his review this week?

Young people across the country have been left without a route into work, education or training. Left doomscrolling in their bedrooms, according to Milburn, without any real hope of building the lives previous generations have taken for granted.

The review was absolutely clear on what needs to be done. Yes, young people need better support. We spend a fraction of the money to help young people into work that we did 40 years ago.

And yes, there has to be a bit of stick with the carrot. If a young person doesn’t engage with the system, there should be consequences.

But Milburn was clear too that for much of the economy, the cost of employing a young person has simply become too high. We have priced employers out of business and young people out of work.

His solution was a targeted cut in National Insurance costs, only for hospitality and retail, and only for young people.

Unsurprisingly, that’s the bit it seems the Government is less keen on.

In 2024, Rachel Reeves used the first Labour Budget in 14 years to raise employer National Insurance contributions.

She did it by lowering the threshold at which pay starts to be taxable, which meant that the effect on lower earners – young people and people working part-time – was more than twice the effect on people earning six-figure salaries.

The result was immediate and crushing. In hospitality alone, around 100,000 jobs were lost. The same story in retail. The high street as a whole lost more jobs in two years than mining lost in the entirety of the 1980s.

It was an unprecedented attack on a single sector.

For 20 years, hospitality has been a rare protection against the Neets crisis becoming a disaster – creating jobs where other sectors were automating roles away.

But consecutive Budgets in 2024 and 2025 all but reversed that.

Three things need to be true for a young person to get a job. First, the businesses which actually employ them need to be viable. Second, the cost of hiring a young person needs to be affordable. And third, you need to be able to hire and develop them easily.

Today, all three are at risk.

Hospitality businesses pay 82pc of their profits in tax, which is higher than any other sector and twice the rate of banks. That figure has gone up significantly in recent years.

The cost of employing a 21-year-old is now 77pc higher than before the pandemic.

And the Employment Rights Act has made employers nervous of taking a risk on people without a track record.

Milburn’s solution of a targeted reversal of the National Insurance increase is modest against the scale of the problem, especially if introduced gradually over five years.

It will be a fraction of the tax grab of the past two years and easily recouped from higher tax receipts and lower benefits by moving young people back into work.

But the word from the Treasury has been that they oppose even this small step towards making first jobs viable.

White smoke in the press and to businesses has been that they are just not willing to make the investment needed to deliver job opportunities and a reduced benefits bill.

But let’s be clear, there is no Milburn review without the National Insurance cut it recommends. We will not get jobs for young people flowing without the high street and the high street won’t start hiring again without costs coming down.

I would estimate, extrapolating the past two years of employment data, that we could see another 40,000 people lost from hospitality alone in the next 12 months unless we start to repair the damage. More than 15,000 of those, statistically, are likely to be young people.

That’s more doomscrolling in bedrooms. More young people’s lives on hold and more benefits for the taxpayer to fund.

I know that the Prime Minister does not see the world this way and I’m not convinced the Chancellor does either.

This looks from the outside like a classic case of Treasury brain, where officials are more comfortable weighing the direct receipts of a tax than calculating the negative impacts, or indeed the positive ones from a cut.

It is the same mentality which led to them taxing away jobs in the first place.

This is a time for courage against intransigence. Downing Street needs to face down the opponents of the review.

Milburn was asked a question by the Government and he gave the right answer. It needs to be implemented without delay.

Allen Simpson is the chief executive of UKHospitality.

data.title: GB News launches British-only rival to Amazon
data.description:
GB News has launched an Amazon rival that will only sell products from British businesses.

The online marketplace, called Shop GB, will allow shoppers to browse and purchase thousands of products, ranging from food and drink to clothing, jewellery and electronics.

While the items can be sourced from anywhere, every seller on the site must be registered and based in the UK.

Shop GB is launching before Black Friday, the major retail event that kicks off the Christmas shopping season.

The site is offering discounts on a range of gaming chairs, while a large blanket printed with black-and-white images of Diana, Princess of Wales, is listed at 41pc off.

Shop GB will sell items from both independent sellers and established national brands.

Fashion retailer 80s Casual Classics, which specialises in retro sportswear popularised by films such as This Is England and The Business, is among the first businesses to go live on the website.

Steve Smith, the founder of Poundland, who is backing the launch, said: “Having spent much of my career building British businesses, I know first-hand the hard work, commitment and determination it takes to succeed.

“British entrepreneurs and business owners are an incredible asset to this country. They create jobs, generate wealth and give people opportunities and we should never underestimate the importance of supporting them.”

Tim Dray, of Shop GB, said: “Shoppers increasingly want to know who they are buying from.

“Every business on Shop GB is a verified British company, so people can shop with confidence and know their money is supporting UK firms and the jobs that depend on them.”

It marks GB News’s latest foray into new areas as the broadcaster seeks to celebrate Britain’s economic and cultural contributions.

The channel last month launched an “all-British” radio station that promises a soundtrack dedicated exclusively to artists from the UK, with programmes including Great British Party Night every Saturday.

But the launch of Shop GB signals that the company – which is owned by Sir Paul Marshall, the hedge fund tycoon, and Dubai investment firm Legatum – is pushing further beyond broadcasting.

A new division, called GB Media, has been launched to lead the expansion plan.

GB News, which launched in 2021, has fended off competition from Rupert Murdoch’s media empire to establish itself as a new player in Britain’s broadcasting market.

But the channel has been beset with controversies over its opinion-led programming and has been hit with an advertising boycott. It has racked up £140m in losses since its launch five years ago.

GB News is facing a fresh challenge from Reform UK, which is using major donations from two crypto billionaires to build its own YouTube-based TV channel.

The venture raises the prospect of a new rival to GB News, though insiders have played down the threat, insisting that the channel is not reliant on one presenter or political party.

data.title: The lesser-known financial benefits of joint accounts
data.description:
Joint bank accounts have traditionally been used by couples to pool their money to pay for household bills and other shared expenses.

However, research by digital wealth manager Moneyfarm shows that almost a third (31pc) of British couples in long-term relationships now refuse to open one at all. Four in 10 view joint accounts as outdated, old-fashioned or even sexist.

Yet despite their declining popularity, joint bank accounts still offer a number of financial benefits – and not just for couples. You can open one with a friend, family member or housemate, too. 

The potential advantages go far beyond making sure you’ve got enough for your next household bill, it could even help out your loved ones after you die.

We’ve spoken to lawyers and tax experts to reveal some of the more surprising financial benefits of opening a joint bank account.

  • Easing probate
  • Inheritance tax advantages
  • Helping to manage finances
  • Advantages for expats
  • What to watch out for

Easing probate

Money held in a joint account automatically passes to the survivor if one of the account holders dies. This can be invaluable if the joint account holder is responsible for covering essential expenses while an estate is going through probate – a process that can take many months. 

During this time, accounts from the deceased will be locked until probate is granted, but with a joint account, the surviving account holder can continue to access joint funds to cover essential expenses.

Duncan Bailey, of law firm Brabners Personal, said: “The surviving partner will need to show a death certificate to the bank to have the account transferred solely into their name. Once this is done, the surviving partner can typically continue using the joint account or regain full access very quickly, without waiting for a grant of probate. This can be a major practical advantage for paying ongoing bills or funeral costs.”

Inheritance tax advantages

For couples who are married or in a civil partnership, transfers between account holders are exempt from inheritance tax.

However, joint accounts aren’t limited to your partner, as you can also open one with a child, other relative, or a friend. In some instances, this arrangement could offer inheritance tax advantages, although it’s not guaranteed and it is essential to seek professional financial advice first.

Mr Bailey said: “Whether inheritance tax applies depends on the specific circumstances, which can sometimes be complex. The crucial factor for inheritance tax purposes is beneficial ownership, which is who actually owns and contributed to the funds in the account.”

One example considered by Mike Warburton, The Telegraph’s tax expert, is whether someone could avoid inheritance tax by opening a joint bank account with their daughter. 

HMRC guidelines suggest that if you simply paid money into this joint account, it would still be “your” money and would form part of your estate on death. But if you did this and made a declaration that the beneficial ownership rests entirely with your daughter, this would count as a lifetime gift to her at that time. 

If you were to survive seven years, the account would fall outside your estate under the seven-year rule. If you died sooner, it may incur a reduced tapered tax rate – assuming it is not covered by the tax-free nil-rate band.

Because the rules are complex, you should keep clear records of all deposits and withdrawals to show who contributed what, in case HMRC makes inquiries later.

Helping to manage finances

Some people use a joint bank account to help manage a relative’s finances, such as paying bills and direct debits, which can be useful when they struggle with online shopping or banking, for example, but still have capacity to be in charge of their own money.

But while this can work informally, it is not a legal substitute for a lasting power of attorney (LPA) should they need something more formal to be set up, warns Stephen Horscroft, of law firm Birketts.

He said: “A bank will typically freeze a joint account if one of the account holders loses capacity. This is because joint accounts rely on the consent of both parties, and the bank has a duty to protect the vulnerable account holder and prevent potential misuse or fraud.

“While essential transactions may still be allowed at the bank’s discretion, non-essential withdrawals are usually blocked until a registered LPA or deputyship order can be provided.”

Advantages for expats

A joint account could also prove useful if you have a friend or relative living overseas who is unable to open a UK account in their sole name because of residency issues.

Mr Horscroft said: “By holding a joint account with a UK-based relative, it can be more straightforward to access UK banking services, pay bills, or receive transfers without the requirement for a UK address.”

However, he also points out that banks may have restrictions on non-resident account holders and anti-money-laundering regulations must still be followed.

What to watch out for

Despite their many advantages, joint accounts come with risks.

Most importantly, you should only ever open a joint account with someone you trust. Each person has equal rights to access and withdraw funds, so if things go wrong, it could be very difficult to recover lost money.

Emma Davies, of law firm Laytons, said: “If either party finds themselves in financial difficulty – for example, bankruptcy or debt – the funds in the joint account will be considered. It is often the case that ownership is presumed to be equal and it can be difficult to prove that this is not the case.

“In this case, it is possible that joint accounts could be frozen temporarily which would limit access to both/all owners – even those who are not involved in the dispute.”

Another important consideration is that opening a joint account creates a financial association on your credit files. If the other person has poor credit, this association could affect your ability to borrow.

Finally, although a joint account can help with access to money after death or incapacity, it shouldn’t replace formal arrangements such as a will or a lasting power of attorney. Always seek professional advice before making significant decisions.

data.title: Water bosses lose bonuses after worst pollution on record
data.description:
Several water bosses will be blocked from receiving bonuses after their companies were awarded the worst possible environmental rating.

One-star ratings at Southern Water, Thames Water, South West Water and Yorkshire Water were all confirmed by the Environment Agency on Thursday.

This means they will now be blocked from paying executive bonuses as part of a government crackdown launched last year that seeks to prevent companies rewarding failure.

The latest ratings were confirmed as part of the agency’s annual performance review. The best possible rating is four stars, which was only achieved by Severn Trent.

The agency announced on Thursday that pollution incidents are still far too high across the UK, with six category 1 incidents reported in 2025.

These are incidents deemed to have had a major effect on the environment or on households, and also lead to a ban on bonuses.

Both Severn Trent and Anglian Water were found liable for category 1 incidents in 2025, meaning they will also be barred from handing payouts to their bosses.

Overall, the EA found that there were 74 serious sewage pollution incidents in 2025, only slightly fewer than the 75 in 2024.

Alan Lovell, the chairman of the Environment Agency, said that the companies awarded one-star ratings had fallen “well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public”.

Ministers are now set to visit a number of sites to interrogate companies’ performance.

Dame Angela Eagle, the Environment Secretary, said she will also be looking at options to strengthen the ban on executives’ bonuses.

It follows the first ever joint report from the Environment Agency, Natural Resources Wales, the Drinking Water Inspectorate and Ofwat, which leaves nowhere for underperforming companies to hide.

In total, there were 2,666 sewage and water supply incidents that took place in 2025, with Thames Water responsible for more than any other supplier: 464.

That was down from 2,801 in 2024.

James Wallace, the chief executive of River Action, said: “Another year, another record low.

“In 2025 almost every water company in England has been ranked as performing poorly, and the sewage kept flowing into our rivers just as it has done for years.

“This year’s figures show that performance is getting worse, not better.”

PM vows to introduce more ‘public control’

Mr Wallace said the latest pollution figures are further evidence that Thames Water, which released 108,000 hours of raw sewage into Britain’s waterways last year, should be put into special administration.

The latest pollution failures have emerged despite £5bn of investment from water companies, which has pushed households’ bills.

The figures come at a critical moment for the water industry after Andy Burnham vowed to introduce more “public control” over the sector.

A spokesman for Water UK, which represents the sector, admitted that improvements were needed.

He said: “Today’s report shows the lowest level of leakage in history. However, the fact remains that the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough.”

Dame Angela said: “Water companies have let the public down time and time again, and today’s report is further proof that root-and branch reform cannot wait.

“People are sick of excuses. I am demanding answer from the companies that are failing.”

data.title: Burnham’s devolution drive to cost bus operator £260m
data.description:
One of Britain’s biggest bus operators stands to lose £260m from Andy Burnham’s move to hand increased powers to local mayors.

FirstGroup, which runs routes across the UK, said the figure represented lost revenue from services it operates in Wales and Yorkshire that are set to come under municipal control as part of the Prime Minister’s local transport crusade.

The UK is set to move away from privatisation to a bus franchising model whereby local authorities take over fleets and depots and then hire firms to operate them.

Graham Sutherland, FirstGroup’s chief executive, said a franchising model set to be rolled out would deliver lower margins, prompting the group to invest in more dependable markets such as coaches and London buses.

FirstGroup’s switch away from the regions highlights the risks of the Prime Minister’s decision to place buses at the heart of his devolution drive.

It was revealed in August that the West Midlands had been hit with a £30m bill after National Express chose to exit local buses completely in response to franchising, forcing the combined authority to buy out 1,400 vehicles and a network of depots.

FirstGroup’s renewed focus on London comes after it quit the capital in 2013 amid a clampdown by Transport for London (TfL) on the value of contracts.

It reversed the move in December 2024 – less than six months after Labour came to power – with the £90m takeover of RATP London, followed last year by the purchase of the Tootbus sightseeing fleet.

The firm now has more than 1,000 buses in London, with revenue this year expected to rise to £350m, an increase of 13pc.

Mr Sutherland said the franchising of buses in West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire and Wales would deprive FirstGroup of around 30pc of its £890m a year in regional bus revenue.

Industry-wide, he said firms faced a slump of £1.5bn a year in revenue in regions that had already announced their intention to move to franchising.

“We will have materially less regional buses in operation. We’ve diversified on the basis that these policy changes were going to impact our regional bus business,” he said.

“We’re still confident that over the next period of tranches we can continue to grow our bus business.”

FirstGroup said it would monitor plans announced by Lord Khan of Tooting for a new public company – Buses for London – which would compete in the capital, where a franchising model already operates but private firms are allowed to operate their own bus fleets and depots.

Mr Sutherland said: “It’s a handful of routes and a small part of the London network at this point. We don’t think it changes much in the short term and we’re confident that the costs and value we provide will stand up in comparison against any operator.”

Industry sources have called the proposals “mad” and “a Sadiq Khan vanity project” that would heap costs on TfL, which is £14bn in debt.

data.title: Burnham accused of dodging scrutiny after ditching press pack
data.description:
Andy Burnham has been accused of avoiding media scrutiny for not taking a full press contingent to two international conferences.

In an unusual move, the Prime Minister chose not to take the normal “press pack” to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda earlier this month, or to Cop31 in Turkey on Thursday.

Guto Harri, the former No 10 director of communications for Boris Johnson, said he had seen travelling to CHOGM with the pack as “loading the plane with a bunch of assassins determined to take out the PM I worked for, but that’s the deal”.

At the last CHOGM in 2024, Sir Keir Starmer took a full press contingent nearly 10,000 miles across the world to Samoa, and held both a press conference and an on-the-record grilling by journalists on the government plane.

Mr Harri said: “You sign up for scrutiny. You agree to be accountable. It’s at the heart of our democracy, and for someone as articulate as Andy Burnham to avoid the press on such an important occasion is not only a sign of weakness but concern.

“I appreciate he does a lot of communication, he does quite a lot of decent interviews, but his modus operandi seems increasingly to be to provide reasons for not answering, not to mention, more importantly, addressing the big questions that a leader needs to tackle, and that’s the one to watch.”

A government source said Mr Burnham had taken part in two pool interviews on Thursday, one in Turkey for COP31 and one in Dublin, as well as a huddle in Dublin where the Prime Minister took 16 questions, including one from The Telegraph.

CHOGM ended up dominating headlines, as the Prime Minister became embroiled in diplomatic clashes over the Commonwealth’s future relevance and slavery reparations.

It is not the first time Mr Burnham has appeared to avoid the press.

In June, the morning after Mr Burnham’s Makerfield by-election victory, he rallied supporters at Ashton Town football club’s ground but did not take questions from the press, nor did he at his scene-setting speech at the People’s History Museum in Manchester just over a week later.

The day he took office, Mr Burnham managed just four questions in seven minutes in an informal, unfilmed huddle with political editors in Downing Street’s Rose Garden before being ushered away for his first call with Donald Trump.

No 10 said it would rearrange the event, but did not, The Telegraph understands.

Government sources said Mr Burnham’s huddle on the first day showed that the Prime Minister’s first instinct was to speak to lobby journalists.

In a similar way to his predecessors, Mr Burnham was interviewed by broadcasters in the run-up to the Labour Party conference in September.

In an interview with ITV at the start of the month, he was asked whether he cared less than his predecessors about what the traditional media said about him. Mr Burnham replied: “Oh, definitely. Well, you see, I left Westminster for a reason.

“I got fed up with commentators deciding things down there, and then the whole world meant to believe what they believe. Well, sorry, the world’s not like that any more.”

Mr Burnham has been interviewed by TikTok and Instagram influencers. However, critics said he was “running away from being asked questions” by traditional journalists by choosing his own interviewers on social media.

Two weeks before he entered No 10, the future Prime Minister took to Reddit for an “Ask Me Anything” session, inviting users to send in their questions.

However, Mr Burnham chose to avoid queries on why the Government was “unable to do major infrastructure projects in this country” or whether he had plans to unfreeze income tax thresholds.

One Reddit user, after his question on “scandalous” student loans was left unanswered, wrote: “Oh Andy, you bottled it. At least we know what the next prime minister’s favourite films are I suppose.”

After his first Prime Minister’s Questions (PMQs), Mr Burnham took to answering social media questions for “People’s Major Questions”, which he called “the real PMQs”.

At the time, Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, told journalists: “I don’t need to use Reddit because I’m happy to take questions from the media.

“Andy Burnham, I’m amazed, was running away from being asked questions. Reddit is easy.”

Matt Vickers, the deputy chairman of the Conservative Party, told The Telegraph: “As mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham never met a camera he didn’t like. Now he’s Prime Minister, he’s gone into hiding.

“The Prime Minister has questions to answer about the tax rises and broken promises piling up on his watch. Social media skits are no substitute for serious scrutiny.

“If he cannot face a room of journalists, how on earth can he face the country?”

Industry sources also warned against the Government’s increasing use of so-called “vanity photographers”, who are employed by No 10 and instructed to take carefully staged photographs of politicians.

Sources told The Telegraph that greater use of internal photographers meant the public only saw a glimpse into the side of politics the Government wanted them to see, in contrast to the images typically taken by the traditional news media.

Some of the most widely distributed photographs surrounding the Budget were taken by No 10 PR photographers, including a prominently used photograph of John Healey’s selfie with his Treasury team.

Sir John Whittingdale, the chairman of the all-party parliamentary group on media freedom, told The Telegraph: “At a time of growing disinformation and social media influence, it is even more important to support professional journalism and mainstream media who can properly hold government to account.

“Access to the Prime Minister is an essential part of that and I hope Andy Burnham will follow the example of his predecessors in regularly making himself available.”

data.title: Britain can’t afford any more quangos
data.description:
Who says Andy Burnham doesn’t do anything of significance? In the last few days, his Government has created “water councils” to supervise an industry that is already collapsing under the weight of over-regulation, as well as a “special health authority” to absorb staff from NHS England.

At this rate, we are well on track for a hundred or more new regulatory, supervisory or advisory bodies a year, each one equipped with generously paid staff and swish London offices, plus the obligatory satellite branch in Bolton. 

This is crazy. The British economy can’t afford all the quangos – we should be abolishing them instead.

If you happen to have some spare time on your hands, and feel like a cushy gig, I recommend applying for one of the new water councils.

Apparently there will be eight of them across the country, designed, in the words of Burnham, to give local people “a real say over what they need from their water company”.

Never mind that we already have one water regulator, Ofwat, with an annual budget of £78m, as well as consultative bodies, such as Water Resources East, not to mention the whole series of financial regulators that all the regional water companies have to deal with.

It seems what we need is just one more layer of oversight.

Likewise, most of us might imagine that the answer to the question of “what do we need from our water company” would be pretty straightforward. Clean water, and enough of it that we can use the sprinklers in the garden over a hot summer, with fewer leaks, and lower bills. But, hey, whatever. It seems we don’t need more engineers, or reservoirs, or any of that stuff. We need a “council” where things can be “discussed”.

Similarly, some of us might have imagined that getting rid of NHS England would mean streamlining the health service. But no.

The Special Health Authority is designed to provide jobs for all the people who might otherwise lose them. It will probably be “special” for them, if not for patients.

Meanwhile, back in September, the Government announced the creation of the OneGov Delivery Agency, due for launch next spring, with a budget still to be determined, while Great British Railways has now been formally launched, with Sir John Kingman bringing all his commercial nous as a former permanent secretary to the Treasury to make trains “great” again.

It probably won’t be long before we see the launch of Great British Steel for all the nationalised metal-bashing assets.

The list goes on and on. It seems like a long time since Sir Keir Starmer – if anyone still remembers him – promised a “bonfire of the quangos”. Instead, the Government is launching new ones at an accelerating rate. There doesn’t seem to be any issue that ministers don’t think can be solved by a task force, a council or a special advisory committee.

The trouble is, none of them is actually going to make anything any better.

There are three big problems. To start with, the costs keep adding up. According to figures from the TaxPayer’s Alliance, 438 quangos received total funding of £378bn in the last full financial year.

Between them, they employ almost half a million people. True, some of that is money that the Government would have been spending anyway, except that it has been outsourced to a separate agency.

But each layer adds costs of its own. There are offices to be paid for, and consultants to be hired, and staff, complete with generous pensions, to be added to the payroll. Each one is, without question, more expensive than if the Government were simply doing the work directly.

Next, it means proliferating red tape. As soon as a new council or agency is created it has to keep itself busy. That only means one thing. It has to keep creating new regulations, and targets, followed by reports on their implementation, and fines for anyone who does not follow the rules.

Finally, all quangos expand. They have to build their empires, just like any organisation, and the only way they can do that is by taking on more people, and interfering even more with whatever industry they are meant to be looking after. We can see that very clearly in their budgets.

Why is Ofwat spending 9pc more this year than last year? It is hard to argue the water industry is 9pc better run.

Or why does the Office of Rail and Road need a 5.75pc budget increase, especially given that most of the rail industry has been taken back into state ownership, so it is hard to figure out why we even need it at all.

No quango in human history ever volunteered to close itself down, or for its funding to be reduced, and there is no chance that any Labour minister will ever demand that it does. Instead, they just expand relentlessly.

The British economy is turning into one giant regulatory body with a country attached.

It is crushing growth, stifling genuine entrepreneurship, and running up huge bills that the economy can barely afford. Even by the standards of this Labour Government, two new quangos in a single week is an alarming rate of increase. At best, they will absorb time and money, while making no positive difference to anything.

At worst, they will make each industry they meddle in even more hopelessly inefficient. The only solution is to sweep them all away – but unfortunately there is very little chance of that happening under this Government.

data.title: The world is facing a new credit crunch
data.description:
High above the streets of Los Angeles, residents of the Beaudry can gaze across the Hollywood skyline, take a dip in a heated saltwater pool, practise their swing on a golf simulator and even send their dog to the spa.

Living in the 64-storey skyscraper doesn’t come cheap. Its 785 apartments command average rents of $4,200 (£3,200) a month, and 95pc are occupied.

By most measures, the $600m building sounds like a property developer’s dream. So why did its owner choose to hand back the keys?

Brookfield, the Canadian asset management giant that built the tower, decided last month that walking away made more sense than refinancing the $360m loan attached to it.

The company said the decision reflected the “entrenched market challenges” facing a city where property values had failed to rebound as strongly as expected. The pandemic hit Los Angeles particularly hard. Office vacancy rates remain roughly double what they were before Covid struck.

But the Beaudry’s troubles offer a cautionary tale about a global financial system being tested to its limits.

The tower is one of the most high-profile casualties of what Larry Fink, the high priest of global finance and boss of BlackRock, has called “the biggest competition for capital I have seen in 50 years in finance”.

For almost two decades, money was cheap. In the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and the credit crunch it triggered, central banks around the world cut interest rates close to – or sometimes below – zero. Easy borrowing kept economies afloat.

But in recent years that reality has been shattered. Inflation has come roaring back after multiple energy shocks and wars, sending interest rates soaring. At the same time, governments have borrowed heavily to fund ballooning liabilities following the pandemic. Add into the pot AI companies spending historic sums, and you have a dangerous cocktail.

“Governments across the developed world are running huge deficits,” Fink warned last month. “That borrowing is now colliding with tremendous demand from the private sector, much of it from technology companies.”

Today, a new credit crunch is setting in. Unlike the global financial crisis, when lending markets effectively froze up, money is still available.

But there is a growing divide between those who can still borrow at affordable rates and those struggling to borrow at all.

The consequences are being felt far beyond financial markets. In Britain, Landsec, one of the country’s biggest property companies, has shelved a £1.5bn redevelopment of Lewisham Shopping Centre in south-east London that would have delivered more than 1,700 homes.

Meanwhile, British Land has paused the next phase of its vast Canada Water regeneration project in Rotherhithe, south London, which was originally expected to deliver 4,000 new homes.

These are far from isolated examples. Across London, at least 42,000 homes have effectively been priced out of the development pipeline, including 12,000 affordable properties, according to analysis by Savills.

Companies are cutting jobs as their debt interest bills rise, and some are teetering on the brink.

The drama is playing out in slow motion, spread over years as companies, households and governments come to refinance loans and face much higher costs than the rock-bottom rates they enjoyed.

We may be at the beginning of this financial squeeze. The question is, how bad could it become?

Debt clock is ticking

Nearly 5,500 miles away from the Beaudry, another debt drama is playing out in Britain.

After almost three years of financial limbo, a decision on the future of debt-laden Thames Water may finally be in sight.

Britain’s biggest utility, which serves 16 million customers, stumbled into crisis after running up debts of around £13bn by 2020. As interest rates have jumped, that debt pile has soared to around £20bn.

The company’s creditors are putting the finishing touches to a “last and final” rescue bid for the stricken utility, after a previous proposal was rejected by ministers in June.

The lenders – a consortium of more than 100 financial institutions from across the globe – hope to persuade a Prime Minister who has pledged greater public control of utilities to give his blessing to the deal.

But sources said time was running out.

Some creditors are increasingly reluctant to provide fresh capital for Thames to meet its day-to-day spending commitments while so much political and regulatory uncertainty hangs over deliberations.

Others are considering walking away altogether and putting their money to work in situations with far less risk, according to another person close to the negotiations. Pimco, the $2tn American bond behemoth, had to be persuaded to stay on board, sources said.

The challenge for financially stretched companies such as Thames is that lenders can increasingly find safer and more attractive opportunities elsewhere.

“There is an ever-growing, unprecedented level of debt financing requirements, so debt investors are asking themselves: ‘I can either put my money into the AI rollout or into water, offshore wind farms or other forms of infrastructure’,” a City source said.

It is an extraordinary choice. Investors are weighing up whether to finance the pipes delivering water to millions of British homes or the data centres powering the AI revolution.

Unlike Thames and other debt-laden utilities whose credit ratings have long languished deep in junk territory, companies such as Meta and Microsoft retain strong investment-grade credit ratings despite enormous spending on AI infrastructure.

The sums involved are staggering. America is on course to pour more than $10tn into AI between 2025 and the start of the next decade, according to the Brookings Institution, a think tank.

As a share of the economy, the outlay will dwarf even the railway and telecoms booms of the past.

Despite growing concerns about the sheer level of borrowing taking place to bankroll the AI race, “much of this debt is being issued by companies with low leverage and rising earnings, meaning they’re well-positioned to support that debt”, JP Morgan’s private banking arm said in a recent note to clients.

Alongside AI companies, governments are the other group borrowing as if there were no tomorrow. Institute for International Finance data show that since the pandemic, global public debt has climbed by $40tn to $110tn.

Governments ripped up their fiscal rulebooks and brought out their chequebooks to shield businesses and households from economic calamity.

Now, demographic pressures are also increasingly weighing on government spending. As Andrew Bailey, the Bank of England Governor, recently highlighted, public expectations of bailouts may not yet have “adjusted back” to pre-lockdown norms.

All of this is making life harder elsewhere.

JP Morgan’s Jamie Dimon, the longest-serving bank chief executive in America, has warned that soaring government borrowing costs and spending on the AI boom risk spilling over into the corporate debt markets, pushing up financing costs for companies everywhere.

“There will be a point where the market will ask for more and more and more, and at one point that’ll feed into corporate debt, corporate credit spreads and things like that,” Dimon said.

In a scramble to avoid a crunch, many companies have been “very aggressive” at reducing borrowings after interest rate rises following the pandemic and then Russia’s war in Ukraine, says Luke Reeve, the head of debt advisory at EY.

But thousands of companies face a day of reckoning. Companies around the world are sitting on a $26.4tn pile of debt, according to S&P Global Ratings, with $13tn needing to be refinanced in the next five years.

In Britain, close to £85bn of corporate debt is set to mature in 2027 alone, according to estimates from EY. Of that, £27.5bn is in the form of bank loans and £57.2bn is owed to the bond markets.

For most, this so-called “refinancing wall” will manifest itself as a sharp rise in borrowing costs.

Even those that moved early have paid a steep price. In 2024, Ocado partially refinanced £500m of debt and saw its interest rate jump from 3.9pc to 10.5pc. The online grocer has since laid off hundreds of staff as it grapples with pressure to cut costs.

For the weakest companies, however, the problem is not simply that borrowing has become more expensive.

It is that investors may refuse to lend altogether.

“Too many businesses have extended and pretended because of the cheap capital,” says Arif Husain, the chief investment officer and head of global fixed income at T Rowe Price.

“We’re going to see a lot more differentiation between good and bad businesses going forward.”

Pressure is already starting to show at the bottom of the market. Interest rates charged on “the worst of junk bonds” are the highest they have been for years, says Husain.

“For the worst companies, that is being reflected in their borrowing costs right now.”

Healthcare, technology and media are the most vulnerable sectors to debt crises, according to S&P.

The scale of the challenges is daunting; companies at greater risk of default have to roll over $61.2bn of debt in 2027, a figure set to rise to $222bn in 2028.

Will they be able to?

“Strong, cash-rich companies can still borrow easily, just at higher rates,” Stephanie von Friedeburg, a senior banker at Citi, told an audience at the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok last month.

“But lower-rated and leveraged companies face a tough refinancing wave that will test their business model.”

A shake-out is already under way.

More than $5bn of debt deals were shelved across the US and Europe last month amid struggles to borrow, according to Bloomberg.

A total of seven companies pulled fundraising plans in October, the biggest spate of postponements this year.

These include AVI-SPL, a Florida-based software firm, which abandoned attempts to raise $690m, and Mesirow Financial, a Chicago-based wealth manager, which put a $175m bond sale on ice.

In Europe, German energy outfit Iqony pulled a €550m (£460m) debt refinancing at the start of November amid subdued investor appetite, just days after a loan intended to finance a €2bn private equity-led takeover of French beauty and wellness brand Aroma-Zone was scrapped.

The borrowers may be very different, but the message from investors is increasingly the same: they are no longer prepared to finance every deal at any price.

And as companies struggle to find willing lenders, another major source of global capital is beginning to retreat.

For decades, oil-rich Gulf states were among the world’s most enthusiastic financiers, pouring their petrodollars into everything from luxury London hotels to American technology giants.

Now, Gulf money is turning inwards. As the Iran war piles pressure on government finances, those same sovereign wealth funds that helped to bankroll Western companies and infrastructure projects are increasingly being called upon to support their own economies.

BlackRock estimates that up to $100bn of Gulf capital could be redirected towards domestic investment in the near term.

Mounting costs to build

As the great wave of credit that washed across the world retreats, things are starting to come undone.

As Warren Buffett said: “You don’t find out who’s been swimming naked until the tide goes out.”

In the UK, the clearest signs of stress can be found in the property market. For many developers in London, the sums no longer add up.

Roughly 96pc of new homes in London are flats. The cost of building them has climbed by 60pc in the past decade, but their value has risen by just 10pc, according to Savills.

Berkeley Group, one of the country’s biggest builders, has said building homes in London is becoming impossible.

This is largely because of rising costs and red tape. Recent analysis by the Centre for Policy Studies warned that government rules had added up to £442,000 to the cost of a London home.

But soaring borrowing costs play a part too. Unaffordable mortgages are hitting demand. Higher mortgage rates are squeezing buyers, particularly those considering flats, and leaving developers uncertain whether they can sell properties at prices that justify the cost of construction.

Beyond property, signs of stress are emerging elsewhere. Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) this month outlined plans to cut thousands of jobs as it grapples with an escalating debt crisis.

The telecoms group is seeking to strip out £800m of costs per year amid growing concerns about its ability to service a £22bn debt pile.

VMO2’s bonds have slumped as investors baulk at the outlook for the company, which is facing fierce competition from broadband start-ups and uncertainty about its ability to buy up smaller rivals.

A record 738,144 UK businesses were in “significant” financial distress at the end of August, according to restructuring company Begbies Traynor.

It said many were “operating with limited financial headroom”. The firm has been producing its Red Flag report, which looks at the health of UK Plc, since 2004.

Spreading the risks everywhere

Even as rising borrowing costs put pressure on businesses, the debt-fuelled AI boom shows little sign of slowing down.

In the past 12 months, AI companies have received almost two thirds of US venture-capital dollars.

A quarter of US investment-grade debt issued this year has come from companies involved in AI, according to Goldman Sachs.

Yet there are cracks emerging there too, as some investors, such as New York City’s $325bn pension system, start turning down AI deals amid concerns about overexposure.

“You’ve really got to be in every asset class, and we are in every major economy on Earth. But now so much of that, sector by sector, market by market, is AI,” Mark Levine, the New York City comptroller, told Semafor, the US news platform.

It’s “a risk that we’re leery of”, said the city’s equivalent of a chief finance officer.

Tremors have begun to appear in the market, with shares and bonds of “neocloud” data centre companies falling sharply in recent weeks.

Governments, too, have faced warning shots that investors will not tolerate their gorging on debt forever. Bond yields have hit multi-decade highs across the West in a sign of unease. The International Monetary Fund has told countries to rein in borrowing urgently to avert a crisis – before it’s too late.

Not everyone will lose out in this new credit squeeze.

Rich investors may find themselves in an increasingly powerful position as companies compete for their cash. Many of those with money looking for a home for it will be “licking their lips”, says Reeve at EY.

For most of us, however, the consequences of a prolonged period of expensive borrowing could be far less welcome. Homeowners will come under pressure, debt-laden companies will cut jobs and governments will surely have to scale back spending, reducing public services in the process.

“Clearly, the people that will suffer most will be the ones that need to borrow the most,” says Husain at T Rowe Price. “The bigger mortgages – [more] higher leveraged consumers – will be most at risk here.”

A new financial world order is emerging, where money is increasingly flowing towards the strongest borrowers and away from those who need it most.

In the face of this new credit squeeze, even a skyscraper full of paying tenants is struggling.

data.title: Nine steps to protect your money from a cyber attack
data.description:
From high street shops and online marketplaces to supermarket fridges, hackers have exposed how fragile our companies and systems are in a wide-ranging wave of recent cyber attacks.

While much of this is out of your control, you can at least take action to protect your money and personal information – and you don’t have to be particularly tech-savvy to do it.

Kiran Fothergill, of Sapphire Security Services, explained: “Think of it like securing your home. You wouldn’t leave your front door unlocked, hand your keys to a stranger or ignore a broken window. The same common sense should apply online.”

We’ve spoken to cyber security experts to explain the simple steps you can take today to make yourself a harder target for criminals.

1. Lock down your most important accounts

One of the first steps you should take is ensuring your most important accounts are secure.

Zain Javed, of cyber security platform Citation Cyber, said: “If you only make one change today, turn on two-factor authentication, particularly for your email, banking and social media accounts.

“This adds an extra layer of security, so even if a criminal steals your password, they will usually need another form of verification to access your account.”

With two-factor authentication, you’ll usually be asked for a second proof of identity when you sign in, such as a code sent to your phone or generated by an authenticator app.

Free authenticator apps include Duo Mobile, Microsoft Authenticator and Google Authenticator. Where available, using an app rather than receiving codes by text message is generally more secure, as text messages can be intercepted or diverted.

2. Don’t reuse passwords

Remembering umpteen different passwords across various websites isn’t easy. But resist the temptation to use the same password across multiple sites.

Doing so means that if one website has a data breach, criminals could try using your stolen login details to access your other accounts.

Instead, you could use a password manager, such as 1Password or Bitwarden, to generate and securely store unique passwords for different accounts.

Jonathan Lee, of cybersecurity platform TrendAI, said: “Pay particular attention to your personal email account. It can be the front door to much of your digital life, because access to your email may allow someone to reset passwords for other critical services you rely on.”

If passkeys are available on websites, these can be even better than traditional passwords. They let you sign in using your fingerprint, facial recognition or your screen lock PIN.

3. Protect your identity

Your personal information is valuable to criminals, so it’s worth taking steps to protect it.

Mr Fothergill said: “Identity protection services can help you monitor your personal information and identify potential exposure or suspicious activity.

“They aren’t a guarantee against identity theft, but they can provide an additional early warning and help you respond more quickly.”

However, you might not need to pay for a specialist service.

Paul Bischoff, of research company Comparitech, said: “Identity protection apps don’t do much that you can’t do yourself, such as monitoring bank accounts and credit. For most of us, these apps are mainly a convenience.”

Instead, you can take some simple steps such as regularly checking your bank and credit card statements for unfamiliar transactions, checking your free credit report for accounts you don’t recognise, and being alert to unexpected password reset emails.

4. Don’t give personal details to AI

With increasing numbers of people turning to AI to ask for advice on everything from medical issues to personal finance, you need to think carefully about the information you share.

Tom Vazdar, of Open Institute of Technology, said: “Treat an AI chatbot like a stranger with a very good memory. Conversations may be stored, read by reviewers or leaked. Don’t type in passwords, bank details, ID documents, medical records or work files.”

Also check your provider’s privacy settings as not all AI platforms handle data in the same way.

Charles Radclyffe, of EA Global AI, said: “Consumer AI tools may use user interactions to help improve and train their models, so users should think carefully before sharing personal information.”

5. Don’t ignore app and device updates

Another simple but important step is to ensure you have turned on automatic updates on your phone, laptop, web browser and apps. It can pay to keep the built-in security features on your devices switched on, too.

Mr Javed said: “Those software update notifications we all put off are actually one of the simplest ways to protect ourselves.

“Cybercriminals regularly exploit known weaknesses in outdated software. Manufacturers release updates to fix these vulnerabilities, but those fixes only protect you once they’re installed.”

6. Guard your bank account

Scammers are finding ever more convincing ways to part people from their cash, which makes it even more important to be on your guard.

Mr Javed said: “The days of spotting a scam because of poor spelling or bad grammar are disappearing. AI means criminals can now write convincing messages and even imitate familiar voices.”

To protect yourself, agree a family code word and ask for it if someone calls asking for money.

Mr Fothergill added: “Criminals are very good at creating a sense of urgency. You might receive a text claiming there’s suspicious activity on your bank account or a telephone call warning that your money is at risk. The golden rule is never to act under pressure.”

This means never clicking on links in unexpected messages or sharing passwords, Pins or security codes with someone who contacts you. If you’re unsure, always hang up and contact your bank directly using the number on the website or through the official app.

Remember, your bank will never ask for your Pin or account details or request you transfer money into a so-called “safe account”.

7. Stick to familiar websites

When shopping online, stick to trusted websites you’ve used before. Criminals can create convincing copies of genuine websites, so check the web address carefully before entering any personal or payment details.

Even if the website has a padlock symbol or “https” address, this doesn’t mean the website is safe.

You should also be wary of adverts and offers that seem too good to be true.

Jamie Akhtar, of cybersecurity platform CyberSmart, said: “Cybercriminals are quick to exploit trending topics, using the excitement surrounding popular games, new film releases and other cultural moments to trick unsuspecting users into clicking malicious links or downloading harmful content.

“If you receive a message promising exclusive access, early releases or special offers, take a moment to verify that it comes from a legitimate source before clicking any links or sharing personal information.”

8. Delete apps you don’t use

Most of us have far too many apps on our phones, so it’s worth having a digital clear out every so often.

The more apps and services you give access to your personal information, the more potential ways there are for it to be exposed if an account or company is compromised.

Art Gilliland, of cyber firm Delinea, said: “Check which apps you’ve allowed to read your emails, see your contacts or access your files. Remove connections you no longer use. Don’t forget that deleting an app from your phone doesn’t necessarily cancel its access.”

It’s also worth reviewing the permissions of the apps you keep and switching off access to your camera, microphone, location or contacts if they don’t need it.

9. Regularly back-up files

Finally, don’t forget to back-up files on your phone or laptop. Doing this means you’ll still have access to important information if your device is damaged, lost or compromised in a cyber attack.

You can do this using a trusted cloud service or an external drive that isn’t permanently connected to your computer.

Mr Fothergill said: “Cyber attacks aren’t always about stealing money. Ransomware and malicious software can also lock you out of family photographs, important documents and personal records.”

Try to back-up your files regularly and check you can restore them if needed.

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: EDF acquires UK rival in push to revive prepayment meters
data.description:
EDF has announced a deal to acquire Utilita, strengthening its position in the UK market by taking on the supplier’s 1.3 million customers.

The French state-owned energy firm announced the takeover of Utilita’s parent group, Luxion, on Thursday in a deal set to be completed next year.

EDF accounts for almost 10pc of the UK energy market and serves more than five million homes and businesses.

It is looking to expand further by acquiring Utilita, which was founded in 2003 and specialises in prepayment meters.

More than 90pc of Utilita’s customers use pay-as-you-go meters, which can no longer be forcibly installed after a government crackdown three years ago.

This stemmed from an exposé revealing that agents working for British Gas were breaking into vulnerable customers’ homes to install prepayment meters.

EDF is understood to be preparing for a greater up-tick in prepayment meters as energy bills surge.

Cornwall Insight predicted on Wednesday that the typical household’s annual gas and electricity costs could climb to £2,166 at the start of next year, a £443 increase from the current level.

The deal remains subject to regulatory approval and the two companies will remain independent until that is granted.

Simone Rossi, the chief executive of EDF in the UK, said: “This is a significant step in our ambition to grow EDF’s UK customer business.

“Together, we will have the scale and skills to keep developing services and support for the households who rely on us.”

Bill Bullen, the chief executive of Utilita, said the agreement “builds on an established relationship between the companies, following the successful transfer of 47,000 of Utilita’s residential customers to EDF in November 2025”.

The deal comes amid warnings that Britain’s household energy debt is projected to rise from £5.5bn to £7bn by the end of the year, with at least two million households struggling to keep up with their gas and electricity bills, according to trade body Energy UK.

Some suppliers and analysts have blamed the suspension of forced prepayment meter installations for the recent increase in energy debts.

Prepayment meters automatically disconnect energy supplies unless they are topped up.

Meanwhile, EDF’s proposed acquisition of Utilita comes amid broader consolidation across the UK energy sector.

Eon’s takeover of Ovo Energy was confirmed just last month, adding roughly four million customers to the German energy giant.

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: ‘Ozempic face’ powers revival of a fading British giant
data.description:
A surprise discovery may have saved one of Britain’s oldest chemical companies from sliding into irrelevance.

Croda, founded more than 100 years ago, was once known as the “mini ICI”, a powerhouse industrial giant with 70 factories in Lancashire and Yorkshire.

But like so much of Britain’s chemical industry, its star has been fading in recent years.

A share price rally during Covid – after it teamed up with Pfizer to produce one of the first vaccines – has been fizzling out, with its stock declining for four consecutive years.

Now, however, a surprise discovery is reversing Croda’s fortunes, giving the biotech-to-chemicals group a new lease of life as a beauty giant.

Croda recently discovered that one of its old chemicals can be used to treat “Ozempic face”, the often alarming facial transformation associated with the fat-jab craze.

For about a decade, Croda had been producing a skin-plumping chemical derived from the root of the plant anemarrhena to limited sale success.

Known as Volufiline, the agent swells the skin by chemically expanding fat cells and is used mostly in body creams.

But after users of GLP-1 drugs complained of hollow cheeks and sunken eyes, doctors discovered that Volufiline can combat the gaunt features associated with rapid weight loss.

The discovery has led to an explosion of sales for Croda, turning Volufiline into a TikTok sensation, in demand from the French and South Korean cosmetics industry.

Steve Foots, Croda’s chief executive, said the success of Volufiline had taken everybody by surprise.

“It had been in our portfolio for a decade,” he admits. “Ozempic coming on the market has created a big opportunity, which we’re capitalising on. It can lead to facial hollowing, but we can innovate around that by plumping your skin.”

Revenue from Volufiline sales jumped 270pc in the first half as more than 150 companies signed up to use it in their products.

Videos tagged #Volufiline have also generated 200 million views on the US TikTok Shop app in 12 months.

It has prompted Croda to lean into its new profile as a key force in the burgeoning TikTok influencer economy, helping send shares up 25pc from their August 2025 nadir.

Unlike Botox, Volufiline is applied as a face cream or in a lipstick-style tube.

Estée Lauder, the cosmetics giant, is hooked and has started selling a 92pc concentrate version of Croda’s agent under the Volufiline name.

Croda has even managed to sell it to the Korean “K-beauty” industry, which pioneered the skin-transforming agents and exports $11bn (£8.3bn) every year.

Foots said that while the fat-jabs windfall was unexpected, it had resulted from a decades-long repositioning of Croda from traditional chemicals into a supplier to customers, including L’Oréal, Procter & Gamble and Unilever, as well as Estée Lauder.

Next up is hair care. Alongside Volufiline, Croda is pushing KeraBio, a synthetic form of biotech-derived keratin, as its next miracle product.

While Volufiline was an existing ingredient that found a new use, Foots said KeraBio – developed at Croda’s research facility in Daresbury, Cheshire – will be its “first big product launch in the beauty industry”.

A similar serum from an American rival sells for £80 a shot.

“It’s solving the problem of repairing hair that’s been damaged through combing and heating and colouring, which breaks the keratin bonds,” Foots said.

“It strengthens your hair in a chemical way by creating new bonds, and stops it from ageing, which is a bit of a holy grail in the industry.”

For Croda’s proud British roots, its re-emergence as a cosmetics force is a major boost for the nation’s chemicals sector.

Foots said that while Croda’s business was driven by breakthroughs made at a plant in Daresbury and a second research lab at its headquarters near Goole, East Yorkshire, still not enough was being done to make the UK a chemical powerhouse.

Only 950 of Croda’s 5,500 employees are UK based, and while it has three British plants, most production takes place at factories scattered around Europe, the United States and Asia.

While the beauty industry may be Croda’s new frontier, the firm is also expanding the plant in Leek, Staffordshire, that was so critical in producing lipids used to deliver the Pfizer jab.

A recent breakthrough by Moderna and Merck in developing a melanoma vaccine that uses the same mRNA gene therapy principles shows the potential of the sector, Foots said.

He said: “We were prominent in solving the biggest medical crisis of a generation with the biggest innovation of its time, which was gene therapy drugs. And it’s still advancing.

“Flu vaccines, cancer treatments. The science is there. It will take time to get to market, but we’re excited because Croda is provital in many of these programmes.”

Croda may be one of the few independent British chemicals groups still standing, but its Ozempic discovery proves there’s life in the old dog yet.
