data.title: Deutsche handled almost $600m of suspicious payments linked to Epstein
data.description:
Germany’s largest bank handled nearly $600m (£455m) of suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, a figure far higher than previously thought.

Epstein was a long-standing client of Deutsche Bank, the country’s largest and best-known lender, after the bank took him on in 2013, despite his 2008 conviction for soliciting prostitution from a minor.

Internal documents show that Deutsche filed suspicious activity reports (SARs) in the US in 2019 identifying $582m of money transfers – more than double the amount previously known.

SARs are confidential alerts that banks must file with the authorities when they suspect a payment or customer could be linked to money laundering, fraud or other financial crime.

The SARs covered payments to women and suspected misuse of charitable donations, the Financial Times (FT) reported.

The value of the transfers is substantially higher than the sum disclosed in August after an investigation by the US Senate finance committee.

Investigators for US Senator Ron Wyden, who wrote the committee’s report, said at the time that Deutsche had flagged more than $250m in suspicious wire transfers flowing in and out of Epstein’s accounts.

The difference could reflect the wider scope of Deutsche’s investigation, which covered about 3,200 payments, the FT said.

The revelations emerged on Tuesday following the leak by whistleblowers of about 15 million internal files from Deutsche.

After he was forced out by JPMorgan Chase in 2013, Epstein followed his long-standing banker to Deutsche Bank.

The paedophile financier’s banker estimated that the relationship could eventually generate $2m to $4m a year from cash transfers of $100m to $300m or more, the FT said, but in reality it was worth far less.

The lender decided to terminate its relationship with Epstein only at the end of 2018, when renewed media coverage drew attention to his sexual abuse of girls and young women.

Epstein was found dead in his US jail cell in 2019.

Shares in Deutsche fell 6pc on Tuesday after the FT’s revelations from the whistleblower leak.

Deutsche has paid more than $200m in fines and settlements for its past dealings with Epstein without admitting wrongdoing.

The anonymous whistleblowers said in a statement that they were motivated by the “public interest”, adding that the bank needed a “complete overhaul in management and culture”.

A spokesman for Deutsche said: “As we said in 2020, the bank acknowledges its error of onboarding Epstein in 2013 and regrets our historical connection with him.

“We have cooperated with regulatory and law enforcement agencies and the US Congress regarding their investigations, and have been transparent in addressing these matters in parallel.”

data.title: Energy bills expected to jump by £443 in January
data.description:
Annual household energy bills will jump by £443 in January to their highest level since 2023, according to a new forecast.

It means the average household’s annual gas and electricity costs would hit £2,166 at the start of next year, Cornwall Insight said on Wednesday. That is 26pc higher than the current level of £1,723, announced in October.

The energy consultancy blamed the painful midwinter hit on the Iran war keeping wholesale gas prices high.

Difficulties getting liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has left European storage tanks at record early-winter lows, prompting a scramble for higher-priced supplies.

Craig Lowrey, an analyst at Cornwall Insight, said: “Events beyond our control have a very real impact on our energy bills.”

Cornwall has raised its forecast from an earlier prediction of a 16pc increase in the January cap, which would have kept the average bill just below £2,000.

Although exporters have found ways to shift crude oil out of the Gulf, there is no alternative for LNG exports – and Iran is still attacking vessels as they pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

European gas prices have dropped to €83 (£69) per megawatt hour from more than €100 in late October but are still more than 160pc higher than before the war.

The hefty increase is a setback for John Healey, the Chancellor, after he vowed to get energy costs down last month.

Mr Lowrey said government initiatives, such as a £100 household energy payment and the removal of VAT from electricity charges “can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East”.

He urged the Government to look for ways to “control how exposed we are to these shocks in the future”, especially by decoupling energy costs from global gas prices.

Ofgem, the energy regulator, is poised to unveil its price cap next Wednesday.

The higher price cap is likely to be a double-blow for poorer households: it will also power even faster inflation, putting pressure on interest rates.

Inflation hit a one-year high of 3.6pc in October, driven by higher petrol prices and a 4pc increase in the energy price cap last month.

data.title: Norway’s oil and gas supplies to plummet in threat to Britain’s energy
data.description:
Britain faces a massive blow to its energy supplies because of a slump in production in Norway.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday that Norway’s gas production will plummet by one third over the next decade and the Nordic country accounts for 40pc of total UK gas supplies.

Ashley Kelty, an energy analyst at Panmure Liberum, said the coming falls in Norwegian output will be “massively problematic” for the UK and drive up household bills.

Norway also accounts for 69pc of all gas imported into Britain, primarily through pipelines that run across the North Sea.

The IEA’s forecast follows a September report from the Norwegian Offshore Directorate, a government agency that monitors the nation’s reserves, which warned gas production may “fall steeply” from as early as 2030.

This is because new discoveries have not been large enough to maintain current production levels and the output of several major fields will soon decline.

Output at Troll, which is the largest gas field on the Norwegian continental shelf and feeds into the UK’s subsea pipelines, “will plateau rapidly post-2026”, it said.

Mr Kelty warned that the UK will be forced to import more liquefied natural gas (LNG), which is far more expensive.

He said: “The Government seems to think that it is all going to be fine because they’re going to build enough windmills.

“But the grid is not going to be updated quickly enough to compensate for that, so it is just going to mean that the UK has to buy more LNG from the US or Qatar, and that is certainly much more costly.”

LNG is more expensive than pipeline imports because the gas must be compressed and then re-gasified.

The UK and Europe will also be competing with Asian buyers, meaning the region will become even more exposed to global price shocks.

The European Union, which also imports large volumes of gas from Norway, is arguably even more exposed than the UK because it has relatively fewer LNG imports, Mr Kelty said.

The IEA said the decline in Norwegian gas production will be so large that overall gas production in Europe will slump by 13pc by 2035 despite the commissioning of new offshore developments in the Black Sea and Eastern Mediterranean.

Norwegian oil production will also fall by around 30pc by 2035, while the UK’s oil output will sink by 45pc.

Mr Kelty said the numbers highlighted the need for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to give the greenlight for Rosebank in the North Sea.

Mr Kelty said: “It shows that it is absolute lunacy not to develop our own domestic resources. Energy security is key. We have access to oil and gas close to home.”

Mr Burnham signed off on drilling at the Jackdaw gasfield last month, but is yet to announce a decision on Rosebank.

Both fields were given the go-ahead for development under the Conservative government but were then blocked by legal challenges from climate campaign groups.

data.title: Labour meddling ‘scaring off Poundland suitors’
data.description:
The Danish supermarket giant behind discount chain Netto has walked away from a potential rescue bid for Poundland, blaming a growing political backlash over the sales process.

The Salling Group pulled out of the bidding process earlier this month as Gordon Brothers, the American restructuring firm, came under fire from Westminster over its ownership of Poundland.

Representatives for Salling Group told Poundland’s advisers that the company was withdrawing as a result of the “political risk and inflammatory commentary” surrounding the situation, according to a City source. Several other unnamed parties had also been scared away by the publicity, the same source said.

Gordon Brothers has been the subject of fierce criticism from Labour and Reform UK MPs amid accusations it has deliberately pushed Poundland towards administration.

A source close to the negotiations said some of the censure “was very unhelpful” because it risked “damaging the process and the outcome”. Some of Gordon Brothers’ most vocal detractors were in danger of “grandstanding”, the source said.

Liam Byrne, chairman of the Commons business committee, accused the American outfit last week of behaving “almost like a wolf on Wall Street, ravaging the British high street”.

Mr Byrne was speaking just minutes after Mark Newton-Jones, boss of Gordon Brothers Europe, was summoned to appear before the committee to answer for its actions.

The Prime Minister, Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, and Reform’s Robert Jenrick and Richard Tice have also weighed in.

Andy Burnham has said the Government was “prepared to find what we can do” to help save the chain, comments that prompted speculation about the possibility of temporary nationalisation for Poundland. Mr Burnham later clarified there was a limit to what ministers could do.

However, Mr Byrne rejected suggestions the scrutiny had been counterproductive.

He told The Telegraph: “Everyone from the Prime Minister to UK Private Capital [the private equity industry body] has urged Gordon Brothers to do the right thing and do what’s right to save a business that employs 30,000 people in the firm and the wider supply chain.

“Anyone who knows anything about retail knows that a successful next step for Poundland depends on the numbers. Recent scrutiny hasn’t changed Poundland’s numbers nor revealed anything commercially confidential.”

A separate Westminster source said the scrutiny had had the desired effect, pressuring Gordon Brothers to release funds and helping to identify several more potential rescue bids. “It has forced them [Gordon Brothers] to behave in a different way,” the source said.

Following the committee hearing, Mr Byrne also accused Gordon Brothers of “extracting millions” from Poundland at the same time as restricting cash and credit access – a decision that risked forcing the retailer into insolvency.

The session was held behind closed doors because the firm had complained about the prospect of it becoming a “show trial”. It denied restricting funding but Mr Byrne said its evidence had been directly contradicted by Poundland’s management.

Mr Newton-Jones told the hearing that Gordon Brothers supported extending the administration deadline to allow several live rescue bids to progress. The next day, Poundland applied for a further 10-day moratorium from creditors so it could pursue talks with those parties.

It is understood Salling could yet return to cherry pick some of Poundland’s shops if its bid for survival is unsuccessful. Close to 20 rival retailers and supermarket chains have expressed interest in buying parcels of stores. Poundland has almost 600 across the UK and Ireland. 

Founded as a small draper’s shop in Aarhus, central Denmark, the Salling Group is now the country’s largest retailer. It operates more than 2,100 stores across six European countries and employs nearly 70,000 staff.

It serves roughly 15 million customers every week and generated turnover of more than 83bn Danish Kroner (€11bn) in 2025. Any profits that are not reinvested in the business are handed to charity.

The group’s Netto brand has hundreds of stores in Germany and Poland. However, it has been less successful in attempts to crack the UK market, exiting in 2010 with a sale of its 700-strong business to Asda. In 2014, Netto returned via a joint venture with Sainsbury’s, but the partnership was scrapped just two years later.

The Salling Group was approached for comment.

A government spokesman said: “Thousands of Poundland workers have their livelihoods on the line, and everyone involved must use this extra time to secure a deal that protects jobs and keeps shops open.

“We will continue to closely monitor developments - our priority will always be protecting workers.”

data.title: China blamed for loss of half a million German factory jobs
data.description:
China has been blamed for the loss of half a million German factory jobs since 2019, as experts have warned that Europe’s manufacturing engine is losing momentum.

German industry shed 496,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute in Dresden, representing a drop of 7.1pc.

Joachim Ragnitz, the managing director at Ifo Dresden, said: “Employment is shrinking in almost all industrial sectors, which is likely a result of declining competitiveness, particularly vis-à-vis China.

“Traditional German core sectors, such as the automotive industry and mechanical engineering, are particularly hard hit.”

The figures follow warnings of a “China shock 2.0” as the world’s second-largest economy pumps out cheap advanced-manufacturing exports that threaten to crush Western industry. China’s trade surplus with Germany has doubled in the last year.

It brings back painful memories of the first shock in the early 2000s, when China unleashed a wave of cheap toys, clothes and manufactured goods into Western economies.

In addition to growing competition from China, the Ifo Institute also blamed vanishing factory jobs on a fresh wave of de-industrialisation triggered by high energy prices and changing demographics.

Europe’s biggest economy has suffered several shocks in recent years, reeling in particular from losing access to cheap Russian gas after the Ukraine war.

As factory jobs have disappeared, hiring in less productive sectors has risen significantly.

The services sector employs 2.2 million more people than in 2019, mainly in health and social care and public administration.

Mr Ragnitz warned that this would spell trouble for the future, as these jobs were unlikely to provide a significant boost to growth.

He said: “The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future.”

Car manufacturers and their suppliers have cut 123,500 jobs since 2019, a plunge of 13pc. Meanwhile, metal products manufacturers cut 115,600 jobs, and mechanical engineering another 64,500.

These three sectors account for 60pc of the job losses.

By contrast, service providers saw strong growth with 391,000 new jobs in healthcare and 357,000 in social services, including nursing homes.

Mr Ragnitz said the country’s ageing population was the key driver of this trend.

Germany has for years had a relatively low fertility rate. It improved briefly for a few years before and during Covid, before plunging again to its current level of 1.3 children per woman.

A fierce backlash against immigration means politicians may struggle to offset such demographic pressures.

Industrial decline has caused job losses in every part of Germany apart from Hamburg. Jobs are also falling faster in the east than in the west, at 8.4pc vs 6.8pc. In Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt, overall employment has even declined.

These are both states where the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is popular, with the hard-Right party winning the largest vote share in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt last month. It also won the state election in Thuringia in 2024.

data.title: Two-tier safety regulations are strangling Britain’s housebuilding
data.description:
The Canada Water redevelopment plan is perhaps the most ambitious construction project in London. The first new London town in 50 years, it promises thousands of homes, millions of square feet of retail and office space, new streets and a town square.

The capital and the economy desperately need this sort of shot in the arm. But the scheme is now in deep trouble.

Rising costs, high inflation and interest rates, and weakening demand have put the second phase of the plans on hold, throwing the £3.6bn development into chaos.

You’ll see plenty of headlines blaming the economic weather, but there’s a truth that nobody wants to confront. The Canada Water scheme didn’t die by accident: it was killed off by government regulation.

The worsening housing market that dealt the coup de grâce was only the last of a series of blows, many of them dealt by government policy.

British Land has been trying to break ground in Canada Water since 2005, only for the financial crisis to hit the pause button. It was restarted in 2014, but it took six years for Phase 1 to begin. Such things take time, but lengthy consultation processes and wrangling held up the project until it had been shaken down for a massive 35pc “affordable housing” target.

Finally ready to go in 2020, Covid lockdowns caused matters to be delayed once again. And just as things went back to normal, in 2023, the Government brought in stringent new fire safety requirements that required the entire development to be redesigned.

The result was to further delay and reduce the viability of the project, leading the affordable housing target to be lowered to 9pc in a desperate last-ditch attempt to save the project.

Some of the new measures were sensible, but the most costly – and least rational – was the requirement for two stairwells in every structure above 18m.

This requirement made Britain an international outlier. In Europe and Asia, mid-rise apartments commonly have a single stairwell, and in France, Germany, Singapore, China and Sweden, the requirements only come in for buildings of around 50-60m, which would have covered a building the height of Grenfell in any case.

Indeed, we know that three central problematic features of the Grenfell disaster were nothing to do with the stairwell. The flammable cladding, of course, which is now rightly banned, allowed a fire to spread that would not have otherwise. A modern sprinkler system would have put out the fire in the first place but was absent. The fire doors would have given residents time to evacuate, but these failed because of poor maintenance by the council.

Beyond some minor adjustments to the cladding, none of these issues would have applied to Canada Water’s apartments, which, like all new high-rises, would have been equipped with sprinklers and brand new fire doors. A failure born entirely of the negligence of the state, and the age of Grenfell, is now being offloaded on to private developments.

In the US, there is emerging research which suggests that restrictive second stairwell requirements there have made construction more expensive and reduced floorspace, without demonstrably improving safety.

In fact, the British Government has done nothing to require existing high-rises to implement the most effective fire safety system – a sprinkler system (estimated to be 99pc effective by the London Fire Brigade) – while making it harder and more expensive to build the modern apartment blocks that would have them by default.

We’ve made new housing too safe to build. By loading excessive safety requirements on to new builds, we are slowing the roll-out of modern fire safety systems and trapping millions of people in unsafe, ageing buildings. It’s estimated that more than a million people live in apartments at risk of fire and as many as eight million live in homes that are in some way dangerous.

When we make it too costly to build safer homes by adding redundant safety measures, it’s those lives that we’re putting at risk.

data.title: Taxman loses out as TalkTalk collapse leaves £2bn trail of debt
data.description:
The taxman is among dozens of creditors facing significant losses after TalkTalk collapsed under £2bn worth of debts, new documents show.

The stricken broadband provider owed around £41m in VAT when it fell into administration last month, according to Alvarez & Marsal.

The insolvency firm said HMRC may recoup some of the money, but warned the exact amount was yet to be determined.

TalkTalk was scooped out of administration by BT in a takeover in October that saved 900 jobs.

The deal was valued at £400m although filings show that the company’s assets were only worth £3m. The rest of the purchase price involvement repayment of TalkTalk’s debts, meeting staff costs and absorbing future losses.

BT acquired TalkTalk following intervention by ministers who were concerned that the company’s collapse could leave tens of thousands of vulnerable customers in limbo.

The broadband provider, which served 2.5 million customers, had been racing to find a buyer as it struggled under a ballooning debt pile.

As well as money owed to the taxman, new filings show the scale of the money owed to investors in the City, as well as industry rivals and other suppliers.

TalkTalk’s largest industry creditor was BT, to which it owed around £125m, largely related to the cost of using the former monopoly’s Openreach network.

It also owes £80m to CityFibre, which operates a rival network, while Microsoft and mobile network Three are among other companies left millions of pounds out of pocket.

Overall, TalkTalk owes more than £300m to unsecured creditors, all of which is expected to be wiped out.

The majority of TalkTalk’s debt – around £1.5bn – is owed to banks, bondholders and other City investors that backed the company.

Ares, the private credit giant that was TalkTalk’s biggest lender and a major shareholder, is understood to have received around £100m as part of the transaction.

However, it is not expected to recoup hundreds of millions more it invested in the business. Private equity firm KKR was repaid the £62.5m it was owed in full.

The administrator’s latest filings underscore how financial troubles at TalkTalk, which was founded by entrepreneur Sir Charles Dunstone, stretch back years.

TalkTalk and Ares first appointed Alvarez & Marsal in November 2023 amid concerns about its liquidity. The following year, Sir Charles and Ares were forced to pump £235m into the company to stave off a looming debt default.

A&M continued to work with the ailing broadband provider, however, with their responsibilities extended to contingency planning this summer as the prospect of a sale became “increasingly more challenging”.

The filings show that TalkTalk received more than a dozen takeover bids after putting its consumer business and wholesale division, Platform X, up for sale. These included one offer that valued the entire company at £565m.

But by September these bids had dwindled, with one from private equity firm Epiris contingent on Openreach writing off around £100m in debt.

On Oct 2, Openreach refused to write off the debt and its parent company BT submitted a rival bid the same day.

In their report, the administrators said: “Following careful assessment, we concluded that this offer was the only option capable of being implemented in the timeframe available, and therefore the only realistic alternative to an insolvent liquidation of the group and the value-destructive consequences.”

BT’s swoop on TalkTalk proved controversial after Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, reserved the right to waive competition concerns using pandemic-era laws designed to maintain public health.

The move triggered complaints from rivals including Virgin Media O2, which branded the deal a “stitch-up”.

The competition regulator has presented a report on the deal to Ms Nandy, who is expected to issue a final decision shortly on whether BT’s acquisition is rubber-stamped.

Alvarez & Marsal and HMRC declined to comment.

data.title: Acutely embarrassing: M&S’s ‘grave’ French error on Christmas jumper
data.description:
In what French speakers would call a fashion “faux pas”, Marks & Spencer has released a festive jumper emblazoned with the wrong accent.

Shoppers have pointed out that its “Christmas slogan crew neck jumper” for men features the word “aprés” [sic], using an acute accent – sliding upwards rather than downwards – when it should be a grave accent, as in “après”.

“Après”, which translates as “after”, is often used in compound terms such as “après-ski”, a term for social activities after a day on the ski slopes. It is among the basic terms covered within the first few weeks of learning the French language, along with “avant”, meaning before.

Adam Parsons, the Sky News Middle East correspondent, wrote on X: “Oh dear M&S. A grave error.” Another wrote on the social media platform: “Not just une erreur, but a M&S erreur!”

Despite the apparent oversight by M&S bosses, the £35 jumper – which comes in the maroon “Bordeaux” colour, has been sold 53 times online so far this week.

Its description reads: “This jumper by M&S features an apres ski slogan knitted into a crew neck design” – with no accent at all.

It continues: “Cut in a regular fit with long sleeves, it’s an easy layer for cosy nights by the fire. The knitted construction adds a soft, textured feel that’s built for everyday winter wear. M&S Collection: easy-to-wear wardrobe staples that combine classic and contemporary styles.”

Other jumpers in different colours used English phrases, such as a bottle green version which read: “Don’t get your tinsel in a tangle.” The Telegraph understands that the jumper is made in Bangladesh.

It is not the first time a brand has made a mistake when using the French language. In 2024, Matalan was criticised when a jumper intended to say “I love you” in French – “Je t’aime” – used “Je’Taime” instead. After journalists told the chain of the mistake, the grey jumpers were removed from shelves.

A spokesman for Matalan said at the time: “Oops! Well done to everyone who spotted the typo. We’ve taken the product off our website and we’re off to brush up on our French.”

A spokesman for M&S said: “We’re aware of the accent faux pas. 

“It was an honest mistake and, thankfully, customers seem willing to forgive our French, with the jumper proving a popular choice this Christmas.”

data.title: Italy puts Revolut under supervision after mobsters move millions
data.description:
Revolut has been placed under supervision by an Italian court after prosecutors discovered that convicted mobsters and money launderers had funnelled cash through the bank.

The digital-only lender, which is based in London, was found by a court in Milan to have “serious deficiencies” in its anti-money-laundering controls in Europe, allowing 24 convicted or suspected criminals to conceal transactions worth nearly €42m (£35m).

The court has put the fintech’s Italian operations under “judicial administration” for one year, a ruling that gives authorities greater oversight of how Revolut operates in Italy.

The issue stemmed from problems at the fintech’s Lithuania-based Revolut Bank UAB, which runs its business in Italy.

A spokesman for Revolut said the company had acknowledged the court’s decision and would co-operate fully with the Italian authorities, adding that its banking services in Italy continued to function normally with no disruption to customers.

The bank is not under criminal investigation, and the supervision process does not amount to an indictment or penalty.

However, the ruling could have broader consequences overseas, with Cetin Duransoy, Revolut’s US chief executive, warning on Monday that the Italian action could harm the group’s American business.

“If you ⁠would have a massive hiccup somewhere, it’s going to have an impact ‌in other places,” he said. Revolut is in the process of obtaining a full US banking licence.

The Milan court said that shortcomings in controls were not isolated incidents but “embedded in a stable management model, repeatedly applied over time”, preventing authorities from freezing illicit funds, according to a 39-page ruling seen by Reuters.

The court has appointed two judicial administrators with oversight and inspection authority, and their powers could be expanded if Revolut does not co-operate fully or if further issues emerge.

Under the ruling, Revolut must execute a 15-point remediation programme and has 60 days to submit an action plan addressing its compliance failures.

The fintech has grown rapidly in the past decade and recently reached a valuation of $115bn (£91bn).

It has faced problems with its internal controls before.

It took Revolut roughly four years to acquire a banking licence in the UK because of concerns about governance. Lenders are usually granted a full licence within 12 months.

Between 2021 and 2026, rival banks reported 256 suspicious transactions involving the suspects, while Revolut filed none.

It was reported in 2024 that the European Central Bank had, after a review, been pressing Revolut to improve the financial crime controls and governance of its EU unit.

The digital-only lender was founded by Nik Storonsky and Vlad Yatsenko in 2015, focusing on prepaid travel cards for spending abroad.

It has since expanded to become one of the world’s biggest fintechs, offering financial products ranging from stocks and shares Isas to crypto trading. The digital-only lender says it has more than 80 million retail customers globally.

The Revolut spokesman also said: “We take our regulatory obligations and anti-money-laundering controls extremely seriously, and we continuously invest in strengthening our financial crime systems, transaction monitoring models and dedicated compliance teams across all markets.”

data.title: Falklands oil contractors down tools after threats from Argentina
data.description:
Contractors working for a British oil driller in the Falklands have downed tools following threats from Argentina.

Rockhopper, the UK-listed oil and gas company, said on Friday that two suppliers had quit in the wake of Javier Milei’s threats to sanction companies drilling off the Falkland Islands.

The contractors had been working on the Sea Lion oilfield, which is a joint venture between Rockhopper and Israel’s Navitas.

A Navitas spokesman confirmed that “they would not perform work on the project in light of Argentina’s activity to impose sanctions, among others, against contractors involved”.

It highlighted a “significant escalation” in aggression by the Argentine government in recent months, specifically against the Sea Lion project.

It comes after Mr Milei threatened in September to sue the British government if the project wasn’t scrapped within a two-week timeframe.

At the time, Navitas and Rockhopper called on Ed Miliband, the Foreign Secretary, to step up support for the project.

Mr Milei, who is a close ally of Donald Trump, claims that Argentina has sovereignty over the Falkland Islands and has declared that the Sea Lion project is “the illegal plundering of our resources”.

His position has been rejected by both the UK and Falkland Islands governments.

Mr Miliband has declared that “the islands are British” and that the UK’s position is “unwavering”.

But the issue has become a diplomatic flashpoint after Mr Trump said he was reviewing America’s position over British sovereignty of the Falklands.

The Sea Lion oilfield, which holds up to 1.7 billion barrels of oil, was discovered by Rockhopper in 2010.

It has since partnered with Navitas to secure more funding for the project.

Navitas said the partnership was in “advanced processes” to replace the two contractors and that “no material adverse effect is expected on the project and its schedules”. Production is expected to start in the first half of 2028.

Navitas and Rockhopper are operating under licenses granted by the Falkland Islands government with the support of the UK Government.

Although the Argentine government has said it has filed criminal complaints against the joint venture and its subsidiaries, Navitas said it is not aware of any formal indictments that have been filed against them.

The Argentine government has also announced the expansion of administrative sanctions against the joint venture and its suppliers.

However, a Navitas spokesman said: “As of the date of approval of the report, no official notice regarding the opening of these proceedings against it has been served to the partnership.”

“The partnership, with the assistance of its legal advisors, is monitoring developments and will act, as required, as it sees fit.”

data.title: Volvo loses £1bn in value as it slashes 2,500 jobs
data.description:
Volvo has announced plans to slash 2,500 jobs after a sharp fall in sales triggered a share price slump that has wiped £1bn from its value.

Shares in the company, which is owned by Chinese group Geely, plunged as much as 31pc after it revealed revenues fell by 23pc in the third quarter.

Volvo announced a 5bn Swedish kronor (£376.4m) cost-cutting plan that will result in around 2,000 job cuts in Sweden and another 500 globally “through natural attrition and by targeted exit packages to employees”.

The car manufacturer warned it may have to take “additional actions” after revenues in China fell by almost 50pc and it was hit by the loss of electric car subsidies in the US.

Volvo issued a profit warning and pulled its annual guidance earlier this month as sales declined.

Hakan Samuelsson, Volvo’s chief executive, said on Friday: “We continue to operate in a very tough environment with strong external challenges: de-globalisation, hypercompetition and climate change.

“The third quarter of 2026 was very disappointing and reflects a year that has become far more challenging than originally anticipated. Our ongoing turnaround plan therefore needs ​a decisive reinforcement.”

Volvo is the latest European car manufacturer to announce sweeping job losses. In July, BMW revealed it would cut 8,000 jobs in an attempt to reduce costs. Earlier this year, Volkswagen said it would cut as many as 100,000 roles out of a total workforce of 650,000. The move is expected to result in the closure of four factories.

Jaguar Land Rover, Britain’s largest car manufacturer, said in September that it would cut 4,000 jobs over the next two years.

Volvo’s revenues in the three months to the end of September slumped to 66.9bn Swedish kronor (£5bn), a 23pc decline from the same period a year earlier.

The car manufacturer also fell to a net loss of 5.7bn kronor (£429.2m) in the third quarter, down from a net profit of 4.5bn kronor (£338.8m) a year earlier.

Volvo, which had bet heavily on electric vehicle sales, said the axing of customer incentives in the US under Donald Trump had dented its revenue.

In 2024, the carmaker scrapped a target of transitioning to selling only electric cars by the end of the decade.

Last month, Volvo said that Mr Samuelsson would leave as chief executive next year, with Klaus Zellmer, the boss of Skoda Auto, due to take up the Volvo chief executive of the Swedish car manufacturer “no later” than October next year.

data.title: The 33-year-old at the forefront of Britain’s defence revolution
data.description:
To see the future of Britain’s defence industry, you have to visit a four-storey building found on what used to be a car park off Old Kent Road. This clean and functional edifice is the biggest new factory in London since the Second World War.

A Union Flag overlooks the factory floor, where 12 machines are silently engaged in turning steel, aluminium and titanium into precision components for jet engines, drones, robots and much more.

Presiding over them is Alexander Fitzgerald, the 33-year-old founder and chief executive of the company, Isembard, which he established in late 2024.

Like everyone who creates a successful business, the T-shirt-wearing entrepreneur spotted a problem and proposed a solution. “What’s happening across every single sector right now – from aerospace to defence to robotics to energy to semiconductors – is that demand is massively increasing, but the supply of manufacturing capacity to make those components is reducing,” he says.

Isembard’s driving purpose is to provide some of that desperately needed extra capacity. The opportunity is all the greater because of a revolution sweeping Britain’s defence industry.

For generations, the sector has been dominated by a handful of large “prime contractors”, such as BAE Systems, which specialise in the slow and hugely expensive production of a relative handful of advanced jet fighters, tanks and warships, designed to stay in service for decades.

But the lesson from Ukraine is that there are increasing – and critical – advantages for countries that can speedily produce an abundance of smaller and cheaper systems, such as drones, then constantly improve and redesign them, and turn out new and better models every few months. This requires a multitude of small and medium-sized enterprises that can compete to be the most innovative and efficient by deploying AI to make an ever-changing array of components as quickly and cheaply as possible.

Isembard is already doing exactly that. Companies send 3D designs for the parts they need, and Isembard manufactures them according to those designs. “We build our own software and AI to make setting up our factories and running our factories really efficient,” says Fitzgerald.

At present, about 95 per cent of components for manufacturing are produced by small and medium-scale businesses. It is an extraordinary fact that the average age of the owners of these companies in the UK is 65 – and that no less than 40 per cent of them plan to retire within five years.

At the exact moment when Europe is rearming – with all Nato countries, including Britain, pledging to spend at least 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence by 2035 – the supply chain for new components is contracting.

Hence, Isembard is expanding rapidly to meet pent-up demand. Fitzgerald opened his first factory last year, and today his company has 18 worldwide – eight in Britain, eight in America and one each in France and Germany.

This growth has been accelerated by Isembard’s unique business model, which allows for franchised factories. All but five of the existing plants are not owned by the company, but franchised to individual operators. The newest, in Swindon, took a mere 90 days to set up, and Fitzgerald aims to get this down to one or two weeks.

Speed and agility are everything. Fitzgerald notes that what has allowed Ukraine to resist the Russian invaders is not one kind of exquisitely engineered drone, but rather a vast and constantly changing array of different models. “In Ukraine, it’s not one type of drone – and 10 billion of them,” he says. “It’s a zoo of different types of drones, at all classes and all stages. Then you need to be able to scale up.”

Fitzgerald adds: “You need a manufacturing base, which is fundamentally a question of, ‘Have you got enough stuff that can make stuff? Have you networked them enough to be more efficient?’ That’s really the core of our business.”

Reindustrialising Britain by reshoring production is, he believes, the key to the country’s future prosperity. “The grand theory of everything is manufacturing because it’s the root of our prosperity, security and purpose,” he says. “I subscribe to the manufacturing dream – that means security and prosperity [depend on] your ability to make stuff.”

Nearby, the computer numerical control (CNC) machines – which have affectionate nicknames such as Cathy and Big Bertha – on the factory floor are playing their part in reindustrialising Britain by turning out the precisely shaped objects that will soon be flying at high speed as the components of jet engines or drones.

The factory, which covers three floors and 160,000 square feet, aims to triple its workforce to 200 by the end of next year. Taking delivery of the hulking CNCs required Fitzgerald to install a bigger loading door in the building, which was previously used as a grocery depot. The machines had to arrive in the early hours of the morning, since there are timing restrictions within three miles of Charing Cross for loads of that weight and size.

Fitzgerald emphasises that Isembard is not a “defence tech company”, but rather a “manufacturing company”. About 60 per cent of its customers are in aerospace and defence, while most of the rest are in robotics.

But Russia is unlikely to be interested in that distinction as its intelligence services carry out their escalating campaign of sabotage and subversion across Europe, including in Britain.

Is Fitzgerald concerned about that threat? “Yes, and I think the Government should be concerned,” he replies. “We have good security protections in both the cyber and the physical side. We’ve had a lot of support from the Government, and from the police and other agencies, as well.”

Fitzgerald has personal experience of Whitehall, since he spent three years as a Treasury civil servant after graduating from Nottingham University with a degree in biochemistry. Earlier, he had also tried his hand at journalism as an intern at City AM.

He enjoyed his time working in the Government, but cannot help remembering: “When I thought I had the right answer for something, it still had to go through six pairs of hands to get to someone to make a decision. That frustrated me.”

He left the Treasury to start a broadband company that amassed almost 100,000 customers before he sold it to Octopus Group in 2022. Fitzgerald founded Isembard soon afterwards, and the company now makes components for customers like Anduril, which manufactures drones and autonomous weaponry, and Oxford Space Systems, which produces the antennae for satellites.

In the past, certain British investors and banks had a fastidious disdain for any businesses linked to defence, some of which were denied financial services. Fitzgerald, who is also an Army reservist, has encountered no such difficulties, and he believes that attitudes have changed. “I think Ukraine has changed that,” he says. “Geopolitics has changed that.”

Something else that has changed is the attitude towards manufacturing in general. One of Andy Burnham’s central priorities is “reindustrialisation” and recapturing the dynamism of former years.

In that spirit, Fitzgerald named his company after the great Victorian engineer, Isambard Kingdom Brunel, though he adapted the spelling of his hero’s Christian name because the original domain had already been taken.

Today, he keeps a black top hat on his desk in tribute to the man whose individual drive and genius powered Britain’s first industrial revolution.

His other inspiration is Lord Beaverbrook, the minister for aircraft production in 1940, who galvanised British industry into delivering 100 Spitfires and Hurricanes every week, making him an architect of victory in the Battle of Britain and changing the course of the Second World War.

“The Air Ministry didn’t like him. He was threatening to resign the whole time, but he got the job done,” says Fitzgerald, who notes that Beaverbrook tripled production in a matter of months by distributing the manufacture of Spitfire and Hurricane components between hundreds of superbly innovative and cost-efficient small and medium enterprises across the country.

That formula saved Britain in 1940. It might yet do the same again.

data.title: How investing in property became ‘an absolute disaster’
data.description:
Climbing on to the property ladder in 2016 felt like a sure-fire route to financial prosperity.

“At that time, there was a queue of nine or 10 people at every viewing in London and afterwards there were effectively auctions outside with the agent,” says Joe, now 37, who works as a consultant.

He purchased a one-bedroom flat in Greenwich, south-east London, for £280,000.

“I felt I had to do it,” he said. “I was at the limit of my affordability and I thought the opportunity would slip away if I didn’t do it. I assumed I would be able to move on quickly.”

After all, the UK housing market had made generations of homeowners eye-wateringly wealthy. Across the 20 years from 1996 to 2016, the value of a typical UK home had surged by no less than 124pc above the rate of inflation, Nationwide data shows.

But Joe did not benefit. After a decade of mortgage repayments and renovations, he sold his flat earlier this year for £270,000 – a £10,000 loss.

The UK property market has turned. High mortgage rates, squeezed affordability, glacial income growth, successive increases in stamp duty and a buy-to-let crackdown are rapidly eroding what has historically been Britain’s favourite investment.

At a headline level, official figures show national house prices rose by 1.2pc year on year in September, but this masks massive variations. The prices of flats are falling across the country. In inner London, sale prices plummeted by 7.2pc, the biggest drop since 2009. Many analysts are expecting price declines to spread across the country in the months ahead.

There is already a wider national downturn that the headline figures mask. Nationwide figures show that, after adjusting for inflation, the value of a typical UK home is now worth less than it was 24 years ago.

Real-terms house prices have shed £63,000 in the last five years, according to the building society, a loss of 19pc since the most recent market peak in 2021.

Lower house prices relative to earnings will ease affordability strains and improve access to housing, says David Miles, a professor of financial economics at Imperial College London. But the transition to a new reality of lower property wealth will bring some economic pain.

Falling house prices hurt consumer confidence and put people off selling. Fewer housing transactions mean lower stamp duty receipts for the public purse.

But it is those who scraped together enough to buy their first homes five to 10 years ago who are suffering the most.

“It is young people, maybe newly middle-class people whose parents didn’t have much money, who get punished for this,” says Joe. “People in their 30s are cash cows for banks.”

He adds: “I pay so much tax. I just don’t really understand what I’m paying in for. I don’t get anything out of the system at all.”

Confidence evaporates

Many first-time homeowners are facing even bigger losses than Joe.

Tom purchased a new-build, two-bedroom flat in south London in April 2017 for £505,000. Nine years later, he is just about to sell it for £360,000.

Including the stamp duty bill he paid in 2017 (before the first-time buyer exemption was introduced), his total cash loss on the property will be more than £160,000.

Tom, not his real name, is able to move on because he had purchased the property without a mortgage with financial help from his parents. But this doesn’t make up for the fact that the money has simply disappeared.

“My father is absolutely furious. I think he’s upset with himself for letting me buy this type of property rather than a more traditional one,” says Tom.

“Most of the money came from his hard work and earnings over the last 50 years. As an investment, it has been an absolute disaster.”

The epicentre of this crisis is in London. Nationally, flat prices dropped by 2.3pc year on year in September. In inner London, they plummeted by 8.5pc.

One very big problem is high mortgage rates. Between February 2022 and October 2023, during the post-pandemic cost of living crisis, the average rate for a buyer taking out a two-year fixed-rate loan soared from 1.56pc to 5.51pc. Rates had been coming down before the war in Iran erupted at the end of February.

Guy Gittins, the chief executive of Foxtons, London’s biggest estate agent, says: “There was a lot of pent-up demand. Then literally overnight the confidence that was building in the market just drained out, almost instantly.”

Two-year rates are now at 4.72pc, roughly triple where they were four years ago. Soaring oil prices and fears of a fresh inflation wave pushed the Bank of England to raise interest rates to 4pc in November, the first rise in more than three years.

Higher mortgage rates have hammered affordability. Before the pandemic, 27pc of a buyer’s monthly income went on mortgage payments on average, according to Capital Economics. This has now jumped to 38pc.

First-time buyers, who are more inclined to be purchasing flats, are most affected because many are already stretching themselves financially.

Yet it is not just first-time buyers being stung by the slump in flat prices. Another group that traditionally made up a large share of flat purchasers was buy-to-let investors. Instead of buying, this group has been selling in the wake of a decades-long buy-to-let crackdown, which has accelerated following Labour’s introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act, tightening regulation on the sector.

Dominic Agace, the chief executive of Winkworth estate agents, says: “Landlords were such a significant part of the flat market since the 1990s. There has been a huge change, a big reorganisation of that sector. Now buy-to-let investors coming to our offices are a rare and endangered species.”

On top of all this, high-rise flats have been embroiled in the building safety crisis that erupted in the wake of the tragic Grenfell fire in 2017. Many homeowners are unable to sell until remediation works have been completed, while those in unaffected blocks have to provide vast amounts of paperwork to prove they are not caught up in the crisis. Many others are also affected by onerous leasehold terms.

Tom’s building does not have cladding problems, but the service charge on his flat has increased from £2,500 per year to £4,500 since he purchased. “The Government is pushing all of this stuff about how much they care about young people and buying new homes. But there is no regulation behind this at all,” he says.

New-build flats already typically come with a premium that is lost on resale and their sellers are often competing with a swathe of other people in the block who are choosing to move at the same time.

Adam Jennings, at Chestertons estate agents, says: “There’s more supply in London than there has been for something like 15 years. That creates an awful lot of choice for people.

“If you are trying to sell, standing out in the market is very difficult unless you reduce your price quite substantially.”

Reductions of 5pc or 10pc on flats are common, says Jeremy Leaf, a north London estate agent. He notes a flat that was first listed at £370,000 was later reduced to £345,000 and has now gone under offer at £330,000.

‘Every deal seems incredibly fragile’

London flats might be on the sharp end, but evidence of the property downturn can be found nationwide.

Adam Horton, founder of Hortons estate agents, which operates outside London, says: “Every deal at the moment seems incredibly fragile.”

One client selling a home in Leicester for around £1m has agreed a sale no less than four times over the past 18 months and each has fallen through, says Horton.

“Each of those was because of funding-related problems. They are stuck in a loop of buyers that just aren’t coming up trumps with the money.”

Another buyer purchased a bungalow in Leicester 18 months ago for £550,000 but had to relocate 18 months later. “They sold it for £500,000. Taking a £50,000 hit was what was required for them to stimulate a quicker sale.”

According to Nationwide, which measures house prices based on mortgage approvals data, values have slumped by 1.1pc since their peak in April. Capital Economics expects they will fall by another 0.4pc in the months ahead.

Simon Rubinsohn, the chief economist at the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors, says: “When you have something that is so built around leverage, what is happening with interest rates has an impact.”

While few economists are forecasting dramatic house price falls in cash terms, the outlook for real values is a different story.

Even once the inflation surge triggered by war in Iran has receded, interest rates are expected to remain materially higher than they were before the pandemic.

A key reason for the heady pace of property price growth in the years before Joe and Tom purchased their first homes was that, for 13 years after the financial crisis, UK interest rates were below 1pc. During Covid, it was 0.1pc.

Miles says: “People came to see getting a mortgage with a 2pc interest rate on it as the new normal. But the world has moved on and away from where we were and it may be that we don’t go back to those days.”

The Bank of England will eventually cut interest rates again, but it is reluctant to take them below 3pc unless there is a major economic shock, says Rubinsohn. “I think the property market is probably in for a more subdued period.”

Geoff Meen, a professor emeritus at the University of Reading, argues that there is another big structural shift that bodes badly for real home values.

“One of the key determinants of house prices is real household disposable income,” says Meen.

As inflation erodes people’s spending power, they have less to spend on mortgage payments. This limits what they can afford to buy.

Real disposable income growth this decade is the lowest on record, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. “That is absolutely crucial,” Meen says.

The Resolution Foundation predicts that real household disposable income will rise by just 1.4pc across this decade. This will be a tenth of the 14pc rise recorded across the 2010s.

“You’re going to have slow growth in house prices unless something really odd happens. It wouldn’t be surprising if there is no recovery in real house prices, at least in the short term,” says Meen.

Economic fallout

In the longer term, lower real house prices will be a good thing for the UK economy, says Miles.

Soaring house prices in proportion to earnings have benefited older homeowners but have blocked many younger people from getting on to the ladder at all, unless they have help from parents who benefited from the boom.

“When you partially reverse that, as we have seen more recently, with house prices falling relative to prices, that shouldn’t be viewed as some kind of economic failure. That is making housing more affordable for people who have been squeezed out,” says Miles.

But this shift will bring some “transitional harm”, he says.

Falling house prices will initially mean fewer transactions, as sellers hold back. “That is unhelpful because it clogs up mobility in the economy,” says Miles. People find it harder to move for work.

There is also a clear correlation between lower house prices and lower levels of construction, says Meen. Developers build based on their ability to sell at a profitable level. Lower real prices therefore bode badly for the Government’s housebuilding targets.

It is also possible that there could be a kind of reverse wealth effect. When house prices are rising, homeowners feel richer and are more able to borrow against their homes, which boosts their spending power. If values are falling, they may be less confident or able to spend.

And there is an impact on the public finances. Lower house prices affect stamp duty, capital gains tax (CGT) and inheritance tax (IHT), says Stuart Adam, a senior economist at the IFS.

While the bulk of most people’s homes are exempt from IHT and main residences are also exempt from CGT, these taxes still apply to rental properties and second homes. A 1pc fall in house prices would lead to £272m in lost stamp duty by 2029-30, a £137m hit to IHT income and £74m less CGT, according to estimates based on Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) figures.

Because stamp duty rates are higher for higher priced properties, the tax is hugely dependent on sales in London and the South East.

The current downturn in these markets has already prompted the OBR to cut its forecasts for stamp duty receipts. In October, it downgraded its assumptions for property transaction tax receipts in 2026-27 by £3.2bn, or 16pc, compared to its March predictions.

Miles argues that, if real-terms prices adjust and homes become more affordable, transactions will rise as the housing market becomes accessible to more people. This could eventually bring higher stamp duty receipts further down the line.

But Joe, for one, has little interest in trying to buy a home again.

“I’m going to keep my money in Isas and stocks and shares,” he says.

“I fundamentally feel that the social contract with millennials is broken. If you don’t have family help, it is almost impossible to get to a position where you have assets, it doesn’t matter what you earn.

“I’m thinking quite hard about leaving the UK. I just don’t really see what the point is.”

data.title: Elon Musk to kill off Tesla’s Cybertruck
data.description:
Elon Musk is to end production of Tesla’s Cybertruck after sales of the controversial electric pick-up proved a disappointment.

The electric carmaker’s chief executive signalled last night that production of the Cybertruck will wind down in 2027, making way for the business to produce more robotaxis at its Texas Gigafactory.

Posting on social media, Mr Musk said: “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

The announcement comes just three years after the Cybertruck first went on sale.

Mr Musk had hailed the three-ton vehicle as “bulletproof” and “apocalypse-proof”, while the company’s website promotes its “ultra-hard stainless-steel exoskeleton” and a range of up to 325 miles.

However, the truck’s high price dampened demand among motorists.

It was initially set to cost $39,999 (£30,600) but the cheapest version now starts at $60,000 (£45,900).

Tesla sold just 11,586 Cybertrucks in the first nine months of 2026, according to analysts Cox Automotive, far below Mr Musk’s previous predictions of 250,000 sales a year.

While Mr Musk had billed the pick-up as the ultimate off-road electric vehicle, the Cybertruck has suffered from a series of mishaps and faults before and after it went on sale.

When demonstrating the truck’s toughened glass during its 2019 launch event, a Tesla executive threw a ball bearing at its window, causing it to shatter.

Tesla has also been forced to issue recalls of the truck over braking issues and other problems, including the vehicle’s trim falling off.

Several trucks have been involved in accidents where they have burst into fireballs after a crash.

Mr Musk took the decision to end production as he attempts to revive Tesla by focusing on AI, robotics and driverless taxis, increasing production of its Cybercab vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots.

The company has launched ride-hailing services in a handful of US cities, while it is planning to build up to 125,000 autonomous electric cabs per year at its flagship Texas plant.

Shares in Mr Musk’s companies have plunged this week after the Democrats swung to victory in the US midterm elections, taking both the House and the Senate.

Tesla’s stock is down more than 12pc since Tuesday, while SpaceX is down 11pc. Mr Musk’s net worth plummeted by close to $80bn in one day on Thursday to around $785bn, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index.

data.title: ‘Tesla of China’ could make cars in Britain as Burnham considers tariffs
data.description:
A company nicknamed the “Tesla of China” is considering manufacturing its vehicles in Britain as Andy Burnham mulls tariffs on Beijing’s electric car companies.

Brian Gu, the vice-chairman and president of Xpeng, told The Telegraph it would be “natural to think about local manufacturing” if sales in Britain hit a certain level.

The comments came as the Guangzhou-headquartered company this week announced plans to launch five new luxury vehicles aimed at British buyers.

Xpeng has been seen as a potential challenger to Tesla, pursuing a similar strategy of hi-tech vehicles packed with self-driving technology, while it has also developed humanoid robots.

Its sleek coupes, such as the LO3, share similarities with Tesla’s vehicles, pitting the Chinese companies directly against Elon Musk’s car business.

At a launch at the luxury Fairmont Windsor Park Hotel on Thursday, Xpeng unveiled the UK version of its LO3 SUV coupe, which it said would start at £32,990 and feature a range of more than 300 miles.

Speaking to The Telegraph, Mr Gu said the company would consider building vehicles in Britain if its launch in the market is a success.

Mr Gu said: “It depends on the success that we anticipate from these launches. We hope to generate a substantial business. And once we reach a certain volume, then it’s natural to think about local manufacturing.”

It comes as the Prime Minister considers imposing tariffs on Chinese electric cars. The EU has already enforced steep tariffs of up to 35.3pc on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) and the Prime Minister has been seeking closer ties with Europe, raising the prospect the UK will adopt similar rules.

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, has been drafting a tariff blueprint and Anas Sarwar, the trade minister, said last month that Britain and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to combat the flood of Chinese EV imports.

Xpeng’s latest UK vehicles will be built in China and shipped to Britain, meaning they would fall foul of any prospective tariff regime. It also produces cars for Europe out of a factory in Austria, although this plant is already near full capacity.

Xpeng’s launch in Britain follows a flood of other Chinese car brands that have swept across the UK market. The Jaecoo 7, made by China’s Chery, was the UK’s top-selling car in September, while BYD, which makes electric cars such as the Seal, has claimed close to 10pc of EV and hybrid sales so far this year.

The European tariffs have prompted Chinese carmakers to shift more production into the bloc to avoid the levies.

Some are also now exploring similar arrangements in the UK in anticipation of potential tariffs here. Chery, whose Jaecoo 7 is known as the “Temu Range Rover” for its lookalike appearance of the British marque, has sealed a deal with Nissan to explore making its cars in Sunderland.

Mr Gu said Chery’s deal was “very much a validation of their success in the UK market”. “If you want to be a leading player, you have to have more local capabilities,” he said.

The Xpeng boss said the company would have to “react” to any new UK rules on Chinese imports. It previously began making cars with Austrian manufacturer Magna in 2025 after Europe brought in its own tough levies.

Mr Gu said: “We have to react to whatever arrangement or regime there is, just like when we reacted to Europe when they announced EV tariffs on Chinese brands.

“We want to keep the current open, friendly and conductive market environment. But we as a company need to react whenever there is change.”

Xpeng plans to build a network of 100 retail outlets and service stations across the UK by the end of 2027. It is planning to open three flagship stores in London and Manchester in the next six months.

The company also announced plans to explore bringing its robotaxi service, known as Yoyo, to UK roads. “London is a very important, key robotaxi market. We also want to see how Yoyo can be tested,” Mr Gu said.

data.title: How we created a contemporary hobbit home
data.description:
When Gail Pirkis and her husband David spent two years scouring Wiltshire, Dorset, Somerset and Devon for the perfect site, and a house they could demolish and rebuild, they finally found what they were looking for on the edge of Dartmoor: a modest 1930s prefabricated bungalow with an extraordinary view. Now in its place is one of Britain’s most thoughtful contemporary country homes: a grass-roofed, granite-clad house that appears to grow from the landscape itself.

“The minute we saw the site on a beautiful May morning, we knew it was what we wanted. In fact, we bought the house without looking inside it,” recalls Gail, co-editor of the literary quarterly Slightly Foxed. The condition of the existing building was of little consequence; it was the setting that mattered. “It had the sense of being in its own private valley with a wonderful view overlooking both cultivated land and wilderness,” she says.

Gail imagined sheltered land, while David wanted a view and plenty of sky. With hills rising behind the house to protect it from the prevailing westerlies, and the land falling away in front before rising again in the distance, the site offered both. Living in London at the time, they were already thinking about a future in the countryside. “I think we always knew that we would like to end up living rurally, and we wanted a chance to build a house that would still be standing in several hundred years’ time,” she says.

For Gail, the move was also about creating somewhere conducive to her work. “I wanted to live somewhere quiet in which to edit, commission articles, plan which books we might reissue and think about long-term plans for the magazine. Our London office is a hive of activity, but not always the ideal place in which to think.”

Vision and design

Having bought the property in 1994, the couple initially submitted plans for an Arts and Crafts-style house, but their application was rejected by Dartmoor National Park. Undeterred, they appointed a new architect and took a different approach. “We planned a more timeless, contemporary house that would sit comfortably within the landscape and permission was granted.”

Their thinking was influenced by photographs of a house in Ireland that had been published in Perspectives, the then-Prince of Wales’s short-lived architectural magazine. Built into a slope and incorporating natural boulders at one end, the house provided a starting point for their own ideas. Working with architect Peter Hall, the couple developed a design shaped as much by the internal layout as by its relationship with the landscape. “We had a fairly clear idea of the layout we wanted inside, but it was Peter who gave external form to the internal layout,” explains Gail. “Crucially, he understood our wish that the house should feel part of the landscape.”

A key part of the vision was to create an uninterrupted connection between indoors and out. The gentle curve of the house is articulated through a series of right-angled corner windows, where the glass meets glass without the need for mastic or a supporting bar. “The corner windows give us the most glorious views,” says Gail. The result is a softened boundary between interior and landscape – an almost symbiotic relationship between the house and its surroundings.

Built into the hillside over two levels, the house has an unusual arrangement, with the upper storey set back from the floor below, creating what are effectively two ground floors. Every window opens directly onto meadow grass. Its boomerang-like curve changes orientation where the kitchen meets the hall, offering differing views from one end to the other. “We drew some inspiration from a Frank Lloyd Wright house in Manchester, New Hampshire, which has deep eaves and where the rooms flow into one another,” says Gail.

Both levels have green roofs: the lower is planted with crocuses, and the upper undulates like a meadow and is sown with wildflowers. Granite forms the exterior walls, while the windows, some sills and the undersides of the deep eaves are finished in oak.

Gail and David deliberately avoided fashionable features. “We didn’t want acres of glass and steel, and fittings that would soon date. Nor did we want an island in the kitchen, bar stools or a boiling tap,” Gail says. Although happy with the design, she admits that some decisions proved less successful. “We went for the cheapest quotation when choosing a builder and with hindsight the project would have been completed much faster and for the same amount of money had we gone for one of the higher initial quotes.”

Considering the environment

The choice of materials was largely guided by a desire to use local and reclaimed resources. The granite was sourced from the spoil heap of a disused quarry about 10 miles away, while oak from trees felled on the land was planked and seasoned for the outbuilding doors, porch bench and cupboards. Inside, the flooring is reclaimed oak and all the windows are double-glazed.

The house’s energy provision has also evolved. “Initially we had an oil-fired boiler and underfloor heating, but we switched to air source heat pumps about 15 years ago,” explains Gail. They’ve since added a wood burner to the kitchen. Their recent application to install solar panels behind an existing granite wall on the land was refused by Dartmoor National Park.

The landscaping was designed to complement the architecture while providing shelter from Dartmoor’s changeable weather. “Here, one needs protection, so the land around the house was landscaped to include existing granite boulders and a ha-ha that separates the garden area from the field below where sheep graze.” Beyond the house are fields, woodland, a small section of moor and tor and a restored lake. “We’ve planted 2,000 trees and now that these have matured, most local walkers don’t realise the house is here.”

Creating an interior for book lovers

With a burgeoning collection of books to accommodate, generous shelving was an essential part of the design. From a hallway flanked by green shelves – where grandchildren are fond of climbing up and down the two sets of library steps – to a staircase incorporating curved pigeonhole shelving, books are never far from reach. “The staircase was built off site before being dismantled and installed in the house, before which we enjoyed practising walking up and down, pausing at the shelves, imagining them in situ,” says Gail.

As Gail says: “Books really do furnish a house.” The collection now stands at 4,000. Alongside Slightly Foxed-published books such as a beautifully illustrated edition of Charles Phillipson’s Letters to Michael, Ysenda Maxtone Graham’s Love Divine and all the children’s books by Ronald Welch, Rosemary Sutcliff and BB (Denys Watkins-Pitchford) the publisher has reissued are David’s mountaineering books, a complete set of Everyman editions of PG Wodehouse, and Gail’s copies of Arthur Ransome’s books.

Just off the sitting room, an alcove serves as Gail’s home office. Lined with books – no surprise – it has a desk beneath a shallow dome with concealed lighting and a secret door leading to a small music room. “It’s a wonderful spot, somewhat inspired by Sir John Soane’s house in Lincoln’s Inn Fields, London.”

However, Gail doesn’t always stay at her desk. “I tend to migrate to the dining room for good light when checking proofs or to the kitchen table where the wood burner is going on colder days.” If she gets stuck on a difficult article, she heads outside. “I tend to go off to the veg patch to do a bit of weeding or take Stanley, our cocker spaniel, for a walk around the land. That usually clears the mind: this is the magic of living here.”
