data.title: The renovation decisions that cause the biggest arguments (and how to avoid them)
data.description:
Renovating a property together should be a unique bonding experience, but anyone who’s ever bickered over a Farrow & Ball colour chart might understand why it can break even the strongest of relationships.

Alarmingly, a recent study by finance company Novuna found that almost one in five couples (19 per cent) seriously considered splitting up – or ended their relationship entirely – amid a home improvement project, while more than half (57 per cent) admitted to fighting over key decisions.

So why can a property makeover cause so much friction? “A home is not only our most expensive possession, but there’s huge emotional investment, too,” explains interior designer Piers Thurston. “Renovation choices are very subjective, and everyone’s vision is different. It’s also much more complicated than many realise, from red tape to liaising with trades, and costs that only emerge once work begins. People often sign up without really knowing what they’re getting into.”

For Valerie Couillard, a renovation project manager who is also trained in mediation, keeping the peace between clients is all in a day’s work. “My role is a bit like that of a couples’ counsellor,” she says. “It can get heated, but I use conflict resolution skills to make sure everyone is heard and brings their ideas to the table. The trick is to work out what really matters to each party and find solutions that tick as many boxes as possible.”

Here we reveal which décor dilemmas are most likely to spark full-scale domestic warfare – and how to navigate them without ending up in the divorce courts…

Paint colours

According to a 2025 study by Houzz, paint shades are the single biggest source of DIY discord, as cited by 51 per cent of respondents. “Colour is so personal,” says Couillard, who founded the Place Between to guide couples through challenging refurbs. “People often get cold feet about bold shades, but using mood boards and Pinterest can increase their confidence, or help them decide if the black ceiling one of them is keen on would look ridiculous or not.”

In moments of tension – or indeed, imminent marital collapse – she says there is usually a way through, with more daring shades reserved for smaller and less-prominent rooms. “Most people are willing to be flexible, so there’s usually a middle ground. With so many thousands of colour options, it doesn’t have to be a deal breaker.”

Thurston says he often looks beyond the paint itself. “I worked with a couple in Surrey on a TV snug, and while the husband preferred plain neutrals, his wife wanted more colour. To meet both their needs, we went for a very understated base colour, and created layering with different textures in subtle sage greens, which pulled in the colours of the beautiful countryside around them.”

Flooring

A close second in the Houzz study, 47 per cent of survey participants admitted clashing over the bewildering choice of carpeting, floorboards, stone and everything in between.

“Flooring is a real Pandora’s box,” says Couillard. “Clients may have their heart set on a type of tile, only to discover that excavation or other alterations are needed, which all add to the cost. There are also technical considerations like thickness, humidity and longevity.”

If squabbles arise, she says one solution is to identify what matters most to each partner and find a meeting point. “Hardwood floors are durable and easy to maintain, for example, but if the other person wants something cosier, you can add rugs.”

While a good designer will never try to sway a couple, Thurston says it is essential they warn them of potential pitfalls. “The most beautiful option is unfortunately not always the most practical,” he says. “If I point out issues like durability and maintenance, and whether someone wants to be sealing a natural stone floor every few years, opinions can change pretty quickly.”

Wall coverings

Wall materials caused rifts for 37 per cent of respondents in the Houzz study, showing that one person’s enthusiasm for flamboyant patterned wallpaper or elaborate tiling can be another’s design nightmare.

“Feature walls can look wonderful, but there’s a risk they’ll end up looking dated,” Thurston says. “I always recommend leaning towards who actually uses the room most, so for instance, if we’re looking at the kitchen, who does most of the cooking or entertaining? It’s really worth considering what the space is used for.”

Couillard says most bust-ups can be avoided if three-dimensional visualisation software is used. “It lets you see how a room would look with wallpaper on every wall, or just one,” she says. “If there’s disagreement over something like a botanical print, the answer might be to use it in a downstairs cloakroom. In my experience, the person who was originally unsure not only accepts it, but comes to love it.”

Appliances

With 22 per cent of couples confessing to feuds over appliances according to Houzz, gadgets such as bespoke wine fridges, built-in audio systems and integrated coffee machines can tip the already-frazzled over the edge.

“One partner is often far more interested in luxury appliances,” says Couillard. “If they really have their heart set on something, let them run with it – the other person can have final say on something else.” She adds that tussles over eye-watering price tags can be averted with a little forward planning. “I always start by asking for a wish list of everything they want if money was no object,” she says. “We work through that and gradually make compromises.”

Thurston agrees that determining which extras are non-negotiable before work begins is vital to prevent future hostilities. “Identify these things early, because when you get to the end of a project, there’s rarely any budget left.”

Worktops

When it comes to doing up a kitchen, few issues generate as much heat as the all-important worktop.

“Marble or natural stone can look amazing, but you have to factor in things like staining and sealing,” says Thurston. “I advise clients to consider overall kitchen design, which means getting samples and looking at them against the rest of the cabinetry, hardware, flooring and even the windows. A lot of the time, any issues are resolved based on what works with the rest of the scheme.”

In her role as a project mediator, Couillard believes in being armed with practical questions: “Who is cooking? Will you want to put hot pans on a wooden counter top, and what’s the risk of burning it?” she says. “I’ll also ask clients if they really want to replace existing marble or granite tops. Changing the cupboard fronts instead can save a lot of money and unnecessary waste,” she says.

Lighting

Even basic decisions over lighting can trigger flashpoints, which Thurston tackles with good old-fashioned compromise. “I’m working with a couple on a country house in Hampshire, and though the husband loves high-tech LEDs, his wife wants a more traditional feel,” he says. “So we’ve incorporated discreet LEDs into Shaker-style joinery around the fireplace and TV that give the look he wants, but still feel appropriate for the property.”

Battles over one-of-a-kind statement lights can be trickier to solve, however. “I’ve had a case where one person wanted a glamorous glass chandelier like you might see in a hotel, but their partner was quite bohemian and very against it,” says Couillard. “So we went for a big rattan pendant instead. That still looks great without being as blingy.”

Budgets

Finally, the thorny issue of money lies at the core of many renovation projects – backed up by Houzz’s findings that 37 per cent of couples lock horns over budgets.

“Usually clients take on good cop, bad cop roles,” says Thurston. “One wants to splash out, while the other is more insistent there’s a finite amount of money.” His solution is a high/low approach. “Some things are absolutely worth the investment, like a sofa which is a strong focal point. But we balance that by going for more cost-effective furniture elsewhere, like in a guest room which isn’t used as much.”

He advocates a healthy contingency pot for unexpected costs, while Couillard – who suggests allowing up to 25 per cent – says extinguishing financial flare-ups is a crucial part of her job. “I bring money up a lot, even though it can be boring,” she admits. “Different levels of finish can mean huge variations in budget, and sometimes I have to ask, ‘Can you afford that?’ I don’t necessarily want the answer. I want them to ask themselves.”

And if those conversations turn ugly? “That’s where the therapy element comes in,” she says. “I take it as a compliment when couples argue in front of me, because they’re not waiting for me to leave before they have a row. They bring it to the table and we deal with it together.”

data.title: How much cash should I have at home – and where should I keep it?
data.description:
The UK Government is urging households to stock up on basic supplies in case of emergencies such as cyber attacks, flooding, fire or power cuts.

Alongside practical items such as bottled water, a wind-up torch, a first aid kit and a portable power bank, the advice includes keeping some cash at home to provide essential backup if card payments or banking apps stop working.

Here, Telegraph Money explains how much cash is safe to keep at home, and the best way to store it.

  • Is it a good idea to keep cash at home?
  • How much cash is safe to keep at home?
  • Where should you store cash at home?
  • How else can I protect my access to money?

Is it a good idea to keep cash at home?

Although cash usage is on the decline in the UK, keeping a small amount of cash at home can be a practical safety net. Recent global events, from cyber attacks and data breaches to widespread power outages, have shown how quickly modern payment systems can break down.

Simon Phillips, a retail and foreign exchange business leader, said: “Most of us take card and contactless payments for granted, and the technology is great – right up until the moment it stops working.”

Last month, a Google system failure caused several banking apps to crash, which resulted in millions of Revolut customers being unable to access their money or use their bank cards, while users of Lloyds Bank, HSBC, Barclays, Bank of Scotland, Natwest, Halifax, Nationwide, Royal Mail and DPD also reported issues.

Keeping some cash at home can therefore be a sensible precaution to ensure you could still pay for essentials, such as food and fuel, in an emergency.

How much cash is safe to keep at home?

As a rule of thumb, you should have enough cash to cover essential spending for two to three days. For smaller households, this might be around £100, while larger households or those living in rural areas might prefer to keep up to £300 at home.

You might be tempted to keep even more, but Harriet Guevara, the chief savings officer at Nottingham Building Society, warned against going overboard.

“Beyond concerns like loss or theft, cash held outside the banking system loses any potential for interest, isn’t protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) and is often not covered in full by home insurance policies,” she said.

Most home insurance policies only cover cash up to a limit, usually between £200 and £500, so check your policy to be sure. Anything beyond that won’t be covered in the event of theft, fire or flood.

Sarah Coles, the head of personal finance at AJ Bell, also suggested having a broader backup plan.

She said: “If you’re worried about having access to your bank, it can make sense to have an arrangement with someone you are close to (and you trust) that you can call on in an emergency, and vice versa. In some cases, if you can’t withdraw money, you can still transfer it.”

Where should you store cash at home?

Cash at home should be kept securely. Yet research from security site Safe.co.uk found that more than two-thirds (67pc) of people keep valuables, including cash, in storage that is not locked.

Anthony Neary, the company’s security expert, said: “Far too often, people are relying on obvious hiding places, such as inside drawers or cupboards, or even out on shelves, which offer little to no protection against opportunistic theft.

“Instead, use a secure storage solution such as a compact home locker or cash box with a lock.”

Storage should be fireproof, as well as heavy or bolted to a wall so that it would be difficult to remove if someone broke into your home. It should also be stored out of sight, away from windows and doors, according to Vlatka Lake, of self-storage operator Space Station.

She said: “Lofts are ideal because they are hard to reach and sometimes require ladder access. If you do go for this option, make sure to store the cash in a sealed container to avoid it getting damaged or mouldy. It should be stored in a dry but well-ventilated area.”

Whatever you do, don’t keep your cash in a bedside drawer or under your pillows or mattress, as these are the first places intruders will check.

Ms Coles added: “There are some traditional hiding spots where burglars will look first, like the freezer, the sock drawer and biscuit tins, so they’re worth avoiding. If you have a lot of books, one option is to choose a book to hide it in. A burglar will run out of time looking for it.”

How else can I protect my access to money?

In addition to keeping some cash in hand, it may also be sensible to be prepared in case your bank experiences an outage.

Ms Coles said that some people will hold two current accounts for this reason, so that if one is inaccessible, they can still get hold of money deposited with a different bank.

Furthermore, the FSCS only guarantees your money up to £120,000 per person, per firm. So if your deposits are likely to go over the threshold, you should spread your money between accounts to ensure that you’re protected.

Similarly, it is considered good practice to keep some of your savings in an easy-access account so it is on hand in case of emergencies. However, this money will not generate the same level of interest as accounts that require notice, so it’s important to only keep what you need there.

data.title: Britain’s biggest pub group sells 300 sites to ease debt pressures
data.description:
Britain’s biggest pub company is selling 300 of its sites to Heineken as it scrambles to cut its multibillion-pound debt pile.

Stonegate, which leases or manages some 4,500 pubs across the UK, is offloading a chunk of its best sites to the Dutch brewer in a deal thought to be worth £300m.

The transaction could go through as early as Monday, according to The Times.

Stonegate, which runs the Be At One, Popworld and Slug & Lettuce brands, will use the proceeds to pay down some of its enormous £3bn debt burden, accumulated through a pre-pandemic expansion drive.

It comes as the sector is ravaged by a firestorm of rising taxes, higher labour costs and soaring energy bills.

Pub closures have outnumbered openings at a rate of nearly nine to one during the past year despite the Prime Minister’s promises to protect the sector, analysis of planning documents showed.

The Telegraph’s Save Our Pubs campaign has called on ministers to ease the tax burden on Britain’s struggling locals, warning that rising costs are threatening the survival of the sector.

The pubs being sold come from Stonegate’s “platinum” collection of its best properties.

Private equity firms Bain Capital and Terra Firma are understood to be among the potential buyers that are still considering purchasing other parts of Stonegate’s portfolio.

The deal will turn Heineken’s pubs division, Star Pubs and Bars, into the UK’s second-largest pub group, beating Greene King. Currently, Star Pubs and Bars runs about 2,350 sites.

The brewer became Britain’s third-largest pub company in 2019 when it purchased 1,900 venues from Punch.

Stonegate’s debt woes stem primarily from its purchase of Ei Group, formerly Enterprise Inns, just before Covid hit and the country went into lockdown.

David McDowall, the former BrewDog director, took over as chief executive in early 2023 and is leading a transformation strategy to turn Stonegate into a smaller but more profitable business.

Part of Mr McDowall’s strategy involves turning hundreds of its company-managed pubs into properties that are rented and run by individual publicans, which has reduced the company’s exposure to higher labour costs.

The company, which is owned by private equity firm TDR Capital, has succeeded in cutting its pre-tax losses, which fell to £53m in the 40 weeks to July, down from £73m a year earlier.

Heineken and Stonegate both declined to comment.

data.title: Hundreds of pharmacies face closure from Labour tax raid
data.description:
Hundreds of pharmacies are facing closure because of soaring business rates, with owners warning that high taxes are forcing them to cut services for vulnerable patients.

Almost half of the 420 pharmacy owners surveyed by the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) said they were considering shutting down their practices because of higher business rates bills.

The trade body warned that pharmacies, many of which are family-run businesses, are unable to offset the higher tax burden by raising prices, which are fixed by the NHS.

The NPA found 55pc of pharmacy operators were considering moving to cheaper premises, raising fears that some rural and coastal communities could be left without a local branch.

Andy Burnham has made lowering business rates for high-street businesses a key pillar of his summer policy blitz, announcing a 20pc reduction for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April next year.

However, pharmacies have been excluded from the relief.

The tax squeeze has intensified since business rates were increased for many properties after Rachel Reeves’s second Budget. Bills have also been affected by the latest revaluation of commercial property.

GPs and NHS dentists, meanwhile, have their business rates reimbursed.

Pharmacies are particularly exposed because most of their income comes from the NHS, meaning they cannot simply raise prices to cover higher costs. Roughly 90pc of pharmacies’ income comes from the health service, the NPA said.

Onkar Singh, who runs 20 pharmacies across the Black Country, Staffordshire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, has seen his business rates bill rise by roughly 20pc to 30pc in the past year. His total bill is now about £250,000.

He has closed two of his pharmacies in the past two years and reduced opening hours across virtually his entire estate. He has also been forced to cut back services, such as offering free medicine deliveries to elderly patients.

Mr Singh said: “The last three years have been the worst period in my 30 years of pharmacy.

“People are having to close a lifetime’s worth of work and effort, and having to close or reduce hours or dip into their pension pot just to keep going for their communities.”

The NPA survey found that 92pc of pharmacies said their rates bill was preventing them from investing in their workforce or renovations. Some pharmacists have warned that their bills have tripled.

Mr Singh said the impact was particularly painful because pharmacies were often being asked to fill gaps elsewhere in the NHS.

He said: “It is frustrating that pubs and restaurants get the headlines, but pharmacies are actually delivering care.

“The NHS accepted that pharmacy did an exceptional job, but in terms of funding and support with business rates we seem to be forgotten.”

The NPA said 44 pharmacies had already closed this year, leaving the national network at its smallest since 2006.

Nine in 10 council areas have lost at least one pharmacy since 2022.

Olivier Picard, the chairman of the trade group, said pharmacies should receive the same rates treatment as GPs and dentists, arguing that they provide an essential health service.

A government spokesperson said: “Pharmacies already benefit from our wider business rates reforms, including permanently lower multipliers and our £4.3bn package to support ratepayers – and the government has increased funding for the sector by £340m this year as part of our shift to bring care closer to home.”

data.title: Poundland owner refuses to pay tax bills as collapse looms
data.description:
The US owners of Poundland have rejected a request to pay tax bills in a standoff that threatens to push the retailer closer to collapse.

The Telegraph can reveal that Gordon Brothers is currently withholding access to £60m in vital funds, meaning Poundland is unable to pay its creditors.

Not only does this include dozens of suppliers, but it has also prevented the business from meeting payment requests from HMRC.

The revelations will raise fresh questions over Gordon Brothers’ stewardship of Poundland as the business scrambles to avoid collapse.

It is understood that Gordon Brothers has not released any funding to Poundland since it provided £20m in two separate tranches a week ago.

This has left Poundland struggling to stay afloat, with management battling empty shelves as unpaid suppliers refuse to provide any new stock.

The turmoil has cast fresh doubt over the sale process, as any potential buyer will be forced to take over a company starved of cash.

Gordon Brothers has already faced fierce criticism from Labour and Reform UK MPs amid accusations it has deliberately pushed Poundland towards administration.

Liam Byrne, the chairman of the business select committee, accused the US outfit last week of behaving “almost like a wolf on Wall Street, ravaging the British high street”.

Industry sources said political scrutiny had not yet served as a wake-up call for the private equity firm, which has tasked Mark Newton-Jones, a veteran retail executive, with running its European division.

“Gordon Brothers are not taking the Government seriously,” said one industry source. “Their actions are not matching their words.”

The private equity firm’s stewardship of Poundland is expected to be discussed when the discount chain’s management meets Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, on Monday.

Poundland is not Mr Newton-Jones’s first brush with controversy. During his time as chief executive of Very Group between 2005 and 2013, staff who were made redundant by the business burned effigies of Mr Newton-Jones outside two sites in Sunderland and Crosby.

A Gordon Brothers spokesman last week hailed the decision to extend Poundland’s administration deadline by a further 10 days, claiming it would bring “additional stability amid an ongoing sale process”.

Talks are still ongoing with potential buyers for the business, including Ireland’s Martin Property Group and Xyra Group Holdings.

However, neither has yet to meet Gordon Brothers’ £30m price tag.

This concerns the repayment of a £30m loan that Gordon Brothers bought for £1 as part of its original buyout.

Failure to find a buyer threatens a break-up of Poundland, which could trigger sweeping store closures and thousands of job losses before Christmas.

Questions have also been raised about the visibility of the two buyers as well as the source of their funding.

It comes after The Telegraph revealed earlier this week that the Danish supermarket giant behind Netto had walked away from a potential rescue offer owing to political scrutiny surrounding the deal.

Representatives for Salling Group told Poundland’s advisers that the company was withdrawing because of the “political risk and inflammatory commentary” surrounding the situation, according to a City source.

A Gordon Brothers spokesman said: “Funds necessary to support Poundland’s ongoing trading continue to be released. In particular, HMRC enjoys a priority position under statute which protects the exchequer in all scenarios.

“We are assessing multiple bids for the sale of the whole company and we are taking due care to ensure that any successful offer can provide the funds required to acquire the business and see it through to sustainable cash generation.”

data.title: Britain’s strange capacity for self-harm is holding it back
data.description:
The stock market listing of AI pioneer Anthropic is being called the float that could make or break the AI boom. Some analysts think that the gargantuan share sale signals lasting momentum, while others believe it is late-cycle hype.

What isn’t in doubt is that Anthropic’s initial public offering is one of the largest, fastest and most concentrated wealth-creation events ever witnessed. Five years ago, this company did not even exist. Today, it is a money-printing machine.

After the sale of 980 million shares at $83 (£63) apiece on Nasdaq, Anthropic was valued at a staggering $1.5tn, creating a corporate payday with few precedents. After a huge 34pc jump as shares began trading on Thursday, the company was worth $2tn.

With around 1.4pc of the shares each, the company’s seven co-founders, including brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei, were sitting on paper fortunes worth around $20bn each even before the share price pop. They have pledged to give 80pc of their equity to charity.

A further 600 Anthropic employees own stock valued at $100m apiece, and thousands more have become millionaires overnight.

But as Anthropic’s engineers and researchers ponder how to spend their newly minted fortunes, Britain is left to lament why something similar isn’t happening here.

After all, Jack Clark, one of the company’s co-founders, is British. Anthropic also has around 200 employees in the UK, the majority of whom are based at the Knowledge Quarter in King’s Cross, north London, alongside rival AI labs and tech giants including Google DeepMind, OpenAI and Meta.

So Britain’s AI credentials are not in question. Indeed, there is a wealth of groundbreaking AI research taking place in the UK, backed by major government funding, our leading universities and numerous cutting-edge tech labs.

In June, two brand-new government-backed AI research labs were launched: one with a focus on creating open-source AI that can run on widely available hardware and another tasked with coming up with new approaches that enable AI to learn without vast centralised computing power.

Yet it is hard to imagine any of this transferring to the equity markets in the way that Anthropic has so spectacularly – or OpenAI is expected to – to similar fanfare next year.

The decades-long, and potentially unstoppable, decline of the London Stock Exchange is obviously part of the reason why the UK has largely failed to produce its own version of America’s AI trailblazers.

So too is our strange capacity for self-harm. A willingness to allow our brightest and best companies to be sold overseas is almost unique around the world.

Arm was our best chance to build an AI champion that could compete on the global stage, but Theresa May allowed it to be sold on the cheap to the freewheeling Japanese investment house SoftBank for the criminally low sum of just £23bn. Ten years later, it is worth £200bn after SoftBank flipped it on to Nasdaq.

DeepMind is another that was let go too soon and far too cheaply. Sold to Google for a paltry £400m in 2014, the company was co-founded by Sir Demis Hassabis, the Nobel Prize-winning Briton regarded as one of the fathers of AI. Meanwhile, DeepMind builds and powers Google’s Gemini, which is locked in a battle for supremacy with Anthropic’s Claude, ChatGPT and other AI assistant tools.

But it’s our obsession with red tape that may prove the biggest obstacle to Britain’s AI ambitions. The difference between the approach that the US and China are taking versus that of our own Government could not be more stark.

While Washington and Beijing bend over backwards to foster the sort of conditions that maximise their chances of emerging victorious in the AI arms race, here some terrified ministers seem concerned only with rushing in more stringent regulation.

In a recent speech, Ed Miliband, the Foreign Secretary, said: “The lesson of history is that we cannot leave it to corporations to put in place the guardrails to serve the public interest.”

Not for the first time, he may be playing to the crowd. Last year, scores of parliamentarians called on the Government to introduce binding regulations on the most powerful AI systems. The campaign is being coordinated by a non-profit organisation called Control AI, and it claims now to have 180 signatories, including Jonathan Berry, the former AI minister.

Labour MPs have been particularly forceful in pushing for tougher rules. In September, the joint committee on human rights, led by Alex Sobel, a Labour MP, said existing UK laws were not fit for purpose and called for a dedicated AI bill to address severe human rights risks.

The House of Commons business, innovation, science and trade committee, led by Labour’s Liam Byrne, followed this with a plea to close gaps in the UK’s AI safeguards.

It doesn’t take a genius to foresee the stifling effect such a stance is bound to have on innovation and growth. Regardless of what many think of the circular financing merry-go-round that the AI industry sits precariously upon, there is a massive amount of wealth and dynamism attached to it that the UK simply is not capable of replicating.

As a result, Britain has almost certainly failed to catch the first AI wave. All is not lost, however. As the many benefits of AI spread, this country has an opportunity to ensure they are captured in the way AI is used throughout the economy.

There are significant opportunities to transform whole industries, from the sort of hard engineering in which Rolls-Royce is a master, to the world-beating frontier drug development of AstraZeneca and GSK.

The UK has many of the attributes to be among the countries that capitalise the most. It has a genuinely first-rate knowledge economy with world-class research and development capabilities in commerce and academia, thanks to some of the best universities anywhere, many of which have created their own leading tech hubs.

There is also a whole generation of brilliant entrepreneurs ready to lead the way, including Sir Demis, whose new company Isomorphic Labs is among those at the forefront of AI drug discovery. It has just raised $5bn in one of the UK tech industry’s biggest-ever funding rounds.

But that’s not enough. Westminster is right to be concerned about the risks that AI poses. The prospectus accompanying Anthropic’s listing contains some terrifying warnings, and there are justifiable concerns that its founders are prioritising the pursuit of growth, profit and personal wealth over safety.

However, there is clearly a balance to be struck between keeping the industry in check and creating the right conditions that foster innovation rather than stifling it. Isomorphic is already valued at $50bn. Persuading Sir Demis that its future lies in Britain, not the US, should be a priority for the Government.

Thankfully, there are ministers who understand all of this. Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, has called for a “noble balance” between safety and innovation. He has also described the UK’s ability to take a more flexible approach to AI regulation than the EU as a “silver lining” of Brexit.

Kanishka Narayan, the minister for AI, cuts a more enlightened figure too, arguing that AI governance requires a trade-off between protecting the public and building “sovereign” capabilities that create economic growth. We must hope these more pragmatic voices aren’t drowned out.

data.title: Financier caught up in row with neighbours over basement golf simulator
data.description:
A financier has won planning permission to dig 4m under his driveway to build a golf simulator and games room, despite objections from neighbours.

Tim Woolford secured permission to install a basement below the drive of his modern home. The underground room will be 13ft 1in deep and have a simulator, bar area and pool table.

Neighbours in Winchester, Hampshire, where homes are worth an average of £1m, say they have environmental concerns about the project and that the works will affect their lives for months.

Residents have referred to Mr Woolford’s home as the “Lego house”, because of its striking modern design, and say it is not in keeping with traditional properties in the area.

Winchester City Council has approved the plans with conditions, despite a planning officer recommending it be refused.

Mr Woolford, his wife and their two children have lived in the house since the coronavirus pandemic and, in drawing up an underground extension, had sought to create an extension plan that would have the least impact on neighbours.

He said: “Our view was that we wanted to do something that would impact people the absolute least as possible. Some of the people that objected misunderstood what would be here when the builders were done.”

Mr Woolford, who is managing director of a finance-management company in London, said he and his wife would still be able to park on the driveway when the building work was completed, so this would not affect the on-street parking.

He said he wanted to build the space for his two sons, who are aged seven and eight, and wanted to install a golf simulator, because they were interested in the sport.

Mr Woolford said: “We have kids that are growing, and it is good for them. We didn’t actually think there would be any discussions about the plans. We did quite a few developments to the house a few years ago, and arguably this has been more contentious.”

He said one of his sons played the guitar and he thought it would be less disruptive to allow him to play in the basement extension – sometimes referred to as an iceberg basement.

Mr Woolford said: “People go into their lofts and convert garages, and I didn’t want to go into the loft and put big windows, and I don’t have a garage to convert.”

He said the process should be reasonably quick and should not cause very much disruption to the neighbours.

He said: “It is actually a quick build. The soil can be taken out within a week. We should be done in about 10 to 12 weeks, so much more minimal than people expect.”

Mr Woolford said the complaints were a “group effort” and they came from houses further down the street, who were not as affected by the works. As well as being 4m deep, the new basement will be 9.5m in width, and 10.9m in length.

Hazel Agombar, who has lived in the street for 20 years, said the house was already referred to as the “Lego house” and she did not think more work should be done to it.

She said: “I didn’t want it to set a precedent of people applying for basement extensions because of the disruption. We have people who are wheelchair users regularly using this street. There is limited parking up the top.

“This is a lovely street, people get on. It’s very green and leafy, and I just thought it was a poor reason to try to change the character of it and try to navigate that disruption.”

Mrs Agombar said that she thought the decision contravened the council’s local plan to make Winchester more environmentally friendly. She said: “It seems to go against the new local plan. It is only one development but it seems like it is starting a precedent. It is for a golf simulation room.

“This is crazy. They have this massive house with a cinema room and garden. If you want a bigger house, maybe you should move if you want to dig up a conservation area.

“The council has allowed a highly intensive carbon footprint development. Digging up that drive is going to be hugely carbon intensive.”

Another objector is Keith Hatter, 79, who is blind and has lived on the street for the last 14 years.

He said: “The main reason was that it involves digging out to about 2.5m of the ground in front of the house, and I am slightly worried that this might have an effect on the soil structure.”

Mr Hatter added: “The second objection I have come to second-hand – because I am totally blind – is that it might interfere with the character. It would involve the trees and general flora in front of the house being removed and have a slightly detrimental environmental effect.”

data.title: Workers fear losing jobs over train delays, warn MPs
data.description:
Workers fear losing their jobs because rail services are regularly late, MPs have warned.

A spate of line closures and cancellations during the summer heatwaves made it impossible for thousands of commuters to arrive at the office on time.

MPs at a Westminster Hall debate said workers were increasingly fearful of the lack of reliable train connections and urged the Government to spend more on rail infrastructure to improve punctuality.

Charlotte Cane, the Liberal Democrat MP for Ely and East Cambridgeshire, said: “One [constituent] in particular has written to say that because their train has been so unreliable for getting to their job in London that their employer is now putting them under pressure.

“They are becoming an unreliable member of staff and their employer doesn’t know when they are going to turn up to work.

“They are also having to make up the time at the end of the day, which means they are getting home very late. It makes it a complete nightmare for them.”

Desperate to protect their jobs, some workers were now considering moving house to be closer to stations with more reliable services, MPs said.

Others are considering giving up well-paid positions in London and other major cities for less lucrative roles closer to home.

Among the worst-hit lines this summer was the route between King’s Cross and King’s Lynn via Cambridge and Ely, the later of which lies in Ms Cane’s constituency.

It suffered three months of disruption, including 900 cancellations after normally damp peat beneath the tracks dried out, leading the ground to become uneven.

James Wild, the Conservative MP for North West Norfolk, which includes King’s Lynn, said people from the town who worked in Cambridge and London had found the disruption intolerable.

He told The Telegraph: “I’ve had quite a number of constituents who have said they’re thinking of moving jobs. They’ve been in tears and incredibly stressed.

“One lady said her husband, who commutes and is self-employed, had been driven to depression and was having suicidal thoughts because he was worried that he wouldn’t be able to provide for his family. It’s pushing people to breaking point.”

Mr Wild said some commuters had opted to drive to Peterborough on the East Coast Main Line, or Norwich, which has trains to Liverpool Street – both an hour away by road – to be sure of getting to work.

He said there were concerns that with the line suffering heat-related disruption for the past two summers, people would stop viewing King’s Lynn as a viable commuter town, which could have a knock-on effect on house prices.

Mr Wild questioned Andy Burnham about the matter in September, when the Prime Minister said he would “convene a rail summit soon”.

Richard Foord, the Liberal Democrat MP for Honiton and Sidmouth, said commuters to cities beyond London had also been affected.

He said restrictions imposed between London Waterloo and the West Country had in one case led a dental hygienist to cancel her 9am appointments “indefinitely”.

Simon Lightwood, the minister for local transport, said he could not rule out further weather-related disruption.

He added that while speed restrictions and closures might be frustrating, the railway’s primary duty was to keep passengers safe.

data.title: White House approves chip sales to Chinese military
data.description:
Donald Trump’s administration approved the sale of advanced AI chips to companies associated with the Chinese military, US records show.

A congressional committee has released documents showing that the White House signed off on almost 900,000 Nvidia and AMD chip sales to China between December and May.

Companies on the sales list include Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu and BYD, which the US department of defence has classified as “Chinese military companies”.

The disclosures come as Nvidia and the Trump administration reckon with the fallout from the Chinese spying affair that brought down Jensen Huang, the former Nvidia chief executive.

The episode has led to a renewed crackdown on Chinese companies accessing advanced AI chips.

But the records show that the US department of commerce’s bureau of industry and security (BIS) approved 21 licence applications for chips that are covered by export controls.

The BIS approved the export or transfer of 879,868 such chips over the six-month period including 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD.

Alibaba was reported this week to have helped set up an AI lab for the Chinese military. JD, another company on the list, has signed a “strategic co-operation agreement” with the people’s liberation army.

The documents show that the chips were listed as “approved but not shipped” and it is unclear whether they were later exported to China.

Chinese AI companies have been making strides to compete with American companies and US export laws are designed to prevent them having unfettered access to advanced chips.

However, the Nvidia saga has focused attention on a series of workarounds used by Chinese companies, including remotely accessing data centres overseas, alleged smuggling and securing special permission from the White House.

The majority of the applications came from Nvidia with a smaller number from AMD. Both companies have been under pressure over sales to China in recent days.

All of the applications said the sales would carry a “low” risk of diversion, meaning they would be unlikely to be used by other customers instead.

This was despite several of the IT companies assigned to install them having been accused of diverting chips, the foreign affairs committee said.

The filings also showed that applications for millions of chip exports had been submitted but not decided on.

This included an application from Nvidia to sell 40,800 chips to New Century Lettal Data Service, a company that The New York Times said was linked to Megaspeed, the Singaporean company at the centre of the Alice Huang spying scandal.

The department of commerce said this week that Nvidia had put Megaspeed on a “no sell” list last year but the records showed the application was made in April this year.

Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu and BYD have all challenged their inclusion on the Chinese military list, with Alibaba and BYD suing the US government over the label.

An Nvidia spokesman said: “The limited shipments we made under the H200 program were legal and authorised by BIS.

“The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have already stopped shipping H200s to China.”

AMD was contacted for comment.

data.title: Swiss face £9bn bill to keep trains running on time
data.description:
Switzerland’s trains are celebrated for their immaculate punctuality. But now the country is facing a £9bn bill to stop its rail services becoming like those in Germany, its erratic neighbour.

The country’s largest railway operator, state-owned SBB, has said its backlog of repairs to tracks and signal boxes rose 12pc last year to 9.5bn Swiss francs (£8.6bn).

If the repairs aren’t carried out, SBB has warned that Switzerland risks “a situation similar to that in other countries” – a reference to Germany, where the formerly clockwork-like train network has become notoriously unreliable.

So far, the Swiss trains are holding the line on their fabled punctuality. This year 94pc of its trains have arrived within three minutes of their scheduled time, about the same rate as the previous two years.

No other major European country gets above 90pc, and many have resorted to using a looser definition of punctuality.

Britain scored 84pc last year. Germany clocked 88pc, but that excludes cancelled trains and defines punctual as within six minutes. Even on that metric, just 60pc of Germany’s long-distance and high-speed trains run on time.

Germany’s decline arose from underinvestment in maintenance. As it tries to play catch-up, large sections of track often have to be closed for repairs, making punctuality even worse.

Switzerland will be keen to avoid that fate.

But SBB is at loggerheads with the Swiss government, which instead wants to spend 20bn Swiss francs (CHF).on expanding and embellishing the rail network.

This could include building a whole new station at Lucerne, at a potential cost of more than CHF 3bn, and a 17-mile tunnel with a potential budget of CHF 800m.

SBB, in a submission to a public consultation, urged the authorities to prioritise fixing the existing network over any major expansion.

Both sides agree, though, that the signalling system also needs a technological overhaul that will cost a further CHF 9bn.

This week SBB kicked off the first CHF 2bn tender for the IT revamp. The full digitalisation of signalling will cost another CHF 7bn by 2045, but so far the government has budgeted just CHF 1bn for this process.

Meanwhile, money is tight for the essential repairs to keep the trains running on time. SBB has said it needs to repair at least 143 miles of track a year, but last year only managed 116 miles.

Funding for its track and signalling work comes from a separate Rail Infrastructure Fund, which is bankrolled by annual contributions from the national and cantonal governments, alongside some hypothecated portions of VAT, income tax and the mineral oil tax. Some of this funding is due to expire in 2030.

data.title: It’s not just Maldon, all artisanal food is a swizz
data.description:
The Great Salt Row of 2026 will become a case-study in business-school seminars about brand management.

A brand is a promise. And Maldon Salt is a great brand, rightly prized by consumers who appreciate its quality and legacy.

Has that promise been compromised by the revelation that it is not all harvested in ancient Blackwater Estuary salt-pans by ruddy-faced Essex artisans, but includes salt sourced from Germany? Not at all. People enjoy Maldon because it is a very good product: to be blunt, it has an exceptional saltiness. Besides, it could have been worse. The admix might have come from the sinister Siberian salt-mines of the Irkutsk Oblast, the ones known to Solzhenitsyn.

What is happening is a long-overdue re-appraisal of the “artisanal” concept. Memory plays tricks, but I am certain I have seen advertisements for Dunkin’ Donuts’ artisan bagels and McDonald’s artisan grilled chicken. Of course, these noxious products are no more “artisanal” than screen-washer fluid (and perhaps even share some taste characteristics). But Big Food knows that “artisanal” gets the attention of the ambitious consumer.

Our fascination with the artisanal is rooted in ever-deeper doubts about the sanitised virtual world and the faceless, unaccountable industries that support it.

Hence, the popularity of sourdough bread, nettle pesto, cold-pressed olive oil, small-batch cheeses and gin distilled in railway arches. Or “natural” wines which often taste horrible, but offer the drinker a refreshing moral superiority as he gets quietly sloshed. These products all seem to offer access to a better world with an authenticity we all crave.

Perhaps a delusional authenticity because “artisan” has no legal definition, but that is not to say it lacks emotional force.

Every recipe in The New York Times’ popular kitchen pages insists on “kosher salt” not because it is important in Jewish ritual (where salt signifies purity), but because it contains no alien additives and comes in large flakes, offering the home cook an agreeable tactile experience in crumbling it into a traybake. “Embodied pleasure” it’s called nowadays.

Who can remember the dinner parties where a little dish of coarse sea-salt appeared on the table, a token of sophistication (and a successor to black pepper)? Or take the recently past fashion of “Himalayan” salt which appeared in large, marmoreal, sweaty pinkish slabs suggestive of the catering at a wholesome outdoorsy sherpa wedding. Himalayan salt is, in fact, mostly sourced from dried-up lakes in the Punjab. But when a powerful claim is made to rusticity, dismal facts only get in the way.

The significance of The Great Salt Row lies in pre-history and ancient history. Salt acquired a mystical character because it is immortal: salt does not rot, so, to the metaphysically minded, it evokes eternity. In Islam and Christianity, as well as Judaism, salt suggests hygiene. You can put it into your bath as well as sprinkle it on your dinner.

You might rub salt into the wounds, but only to prevent infection. Salt was once so cash-valuable, it was part of a Roman legionnaire’s pay packet: “salary” comes from the Latin for salt.

But beyond all of this, there is something contemporary and immediate in The Great Salt Row. It is, in fact, about terroir, the word French wine-makers use to describe how the soil and the weather combine to create locality, making tastes that are specific to one region, even to a single vineyard.

Globalisation has robbed us of terroir. This is the fundamental appeal of “artisanal”: the word promises authenticity and locality. William Blake’s most famous line was about seeing the world in a grain of sand. You can see the world in a handful of salt.

data.title: BBC scraps Room on the Broom over Walliams abuse allegations
data.description:
The BBC has removed an adaptation of Dame Julia Donaldson’s children’s book Room On The Broom featuring David Walliams.

The broadcaster withdrew the animated 2012 film from platforms such as iPlayer as part of a review of “all material” featuring and written by the comedian following the publication of sex abuse allegations.

Walliams, 55, a children’s author and former Britain’s Got Talent (BGT) judge, was named as part of an alleged sexual misconduct investigation by The Guardian and ITV News on Tuesday.

One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as “sexual assault”, while several women accused him of “grooming” them when they were teenagers. Walliams denies any wrongdoing.

On Friday, the Metropolitan Police said it had received a number of non-recent “serious” sex offence allegations against him “in recent days”.

Earlier in the week, the BBC said it was carrying out a content review on its platforms and was in the process of “removing” some.

In Room On The Broom, Walliams voices a frog, alongside Gillian Anderson as a witch and Simon Pegg as the narrator.

His character has just three lines in the 30-minute film, along with some “ribbits”.

In one line, his character says: “I am a frog, as clean as can be. Is there room on the broom for a frog like me?”

A BBC spokesman said: “These are serious allegations. As such, the BBC is looking carefully at all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms. We are in the process of removing some programmes, including Little Britain, whilst this review is under way.”

Walliams rose to fame working alongside Matt Lucas on the BBC sketch comedy series Little Britain, which ran from 2003 until 2006.

They then created and starred in Come Fly With Me, which aired on the BBC for one season in 2010.

Both shows are currently unavailable on iPlayer, as is a 2020 episode of Who Do You Think You Are? featuring Walliams.

Adaptations of his best-selling children’s books, including Gangsta Granny and Billionaire Boy, are also unavailable on the service.

Channel 4 and Sky also axe Walliams content

Other broadcasters have also removed programming featuring Walliams from their streaming services.

Channel 4 has taken down episodes of 8 Out Of 10 Cats Does Countdown and the 2021 special Chitty Flies Again with Walliams.

Sky also removed Walliams’s work from its platform and dropped the distribution of the upcoming film Fing! based on his 2019 children’s book.

In a statement, a Sky spokesman said: “The allegations made against David Walliams are extremely serious. We have notified the producers of the film of our intention to exit our position as the UK and Ireland licensee of Fing!

“We have already removed content which features him from our platforms.”

Angel Studios confirmed it would still release the film in the US, but a cameo featuring Walliams would be removed and he would not take part in its promotion.

Walliams has not yet responded to Tuesday’s reports in The Guardian or ITV News.

But in a letter understood to have been sent several months ago to journalists working on the investigations, he denied being a “sexual predator”.

Walliams said he recognised he “behaved thoughtlessly” at times, and regretted not taking people’s feelings “properly into account”, but insisted he had not broken the law.

The ITV and The Guardian reports about Walliams followed his unsuccessful attempts to seek an injunction to prevent the media revealing his identity – with his lawyers arguing there was a risk he would take his own life after two previous suicide attempts.

Several sources alleged inappropriate behaviour towards women at the prime-time show BGT, where Walliams served as a judge from 2012 to 2022, and at his publisher HarperCollins, which dropped him last year.

The allegations also led to Walliams being dropped by his literary agency, Independent Talent Group.
